title: Beyond speeches
author: none@none.com (Sajjad Hussain Changezi)
content:
EACH budget session follows a familiar ritual. Finance ministers announce ‘people-friendly’ budgets in the national and provincial assemblies. Social sectors are labelled priorities. Billions allocated to education and health are invoked as proof of the government’s concern for human development. The amounts are large enough to overwhelm the citizenry. But a reading of the annual budget statements for FY2026-27 on the websites of the federal and provincial finance ministries tells a complicated story.

I’ll focus here on the national and provincial education budgets, with the exception of the KP budget, where the numbers seem to be underreported. I’ll judge these budgets against three questions: did education receive more funds this year than it did last year; can this year’s money buy more after adjustment for inflation, and has education’s share of the overall government budget increased?

Starting with a year-on-year comparison of the nominal allocated budgets, Punjab’s education allocation has fallen from Rs811.1bn in 2025-26 to Rs789.2bn in 2026-27, a reduction of 2.7 per cent. Sindh’s allocation has similarly declined from Rs654.2bn to Rs635.8bn, by 2.8pc. Balo­ch­istan’s allocation has increased from Rs156.5bn to Rs171.2bn. The federal allocation has increased from Rs168.5bn to Rs194.1bn. In the case of Punjab and Sindh, suffice it to say that a budget that is lower in rupees than the previous year’s budget is a cut.

The second question concerns the comparable purchasing power of these budgets: what can the money actually buy this year? The average national consumer price inflation in FY2025-26 was 7.05pc. In other words, what you could buy with Rs100 in 2025-26, you can only buy with Rs107 in 2026-27. Building material, electricity, transport, textbooks, digital equipment and basic services have all become more expensive. When current allocations are expressed in 2025-26 prices, Punjab’s Rs789.2bn is worth around Rs737.3bn and Sindh’s Rs635.8bn comes down 
to around Rs593.9bn. In real terms, Punjab’s education resources have declined by about 9.1pc and Sindh’s by 9.2pc.

Bold claims hide the reality of education spending.

Third, and ultimately, the criterion is education’s share of the total government budget. In Balochistan, education’s share declines from 16pc to 15.7pc of the total provincial budget. Punjab’s share falls from 15.2pc to 13.4pc. In Sindh, it drops from 19pc to 17.8pc. Federally, it rises from 0.71pc to 0.77pc but still amounts to less than Rs1 out of every Rs100 spent by the federation.

These numbers reveal choices. Budget statements show what governments prioritise when resources are limited. They show whether an education emergency is reflected in financial planning or is confined to speeches. Pakistan has declared educational emergencies for years. Yet millions of children remain out of school. Learning poverty is widespread. Schools in remote communities lack teachers, safe buildings and basic facilities. Girls face further barriers, especially when moving from primary to middle and secondary school. An emergency can’t be declared in a vacuum. It must be funded sufficiently.

There is another structural problem in how education budgets are presented. They are largely gender-blind. Budget documents report aggregate education allocations but offer little clarity on how much is directed towards girls. Illiteracy is an intergenerational problem. Many out-of-school children grow up in families where their parents, particularly their mothers, were denied an education. A mother who has not had the opportunity to attend school may find it harder to navigate official systems, ob­­tain information, su­­­p­po­­rt learning at home, demand ac­­count­ab­ility or keep a child enrolled when ho­-

u­sehold re­­sources are under pressure. This is not a matter of individual failure. It is how educational exclusion can reproduce itself across generations. Girls’ education cannot remain a peripheral concern. Women’s education and empowerment are closely linked with better child health, school attendance, nutrition, household income and civic participation. If we are serious about long-term sustainable growth, girls’ education must be treated as an economic investment.

This year’s budgets offer an uneven answer. Punjab and Sindh are allocating fewer funds than last year, even before the inflation adjustment. Balochistan has increased its education allocation, but its share of the overall budget has fallen. The federation’s allocation shows an increase but education still receives less than 1pc of the total federal expenditure. Until budget statements show sustained increases in education’s share, allocations that retain their value against inflation and transparent spending on girls and the most excluded children, applause during budget speeches will remain louder than the commitment claimed.

The writer is a development professional working at Tabadlab.

title: Pitfalls of referendum
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
THE plot thickens. What the ubiquitous interior minister said makes at least one thing clear: restructuring the existing administrative framework is inevitable. It was apparent that he was not voicing the view of the civilian dispensation but that of the powers that be. “New administrative units will have to be created. No one can stop it,” he declared. There was also a clear hint that a referendum might be held to determine the “will of the people” on the issue.

Mohsin Naqvi, a man of all seasons, appears to have been handed yet another political project — added to a portfolio that already ranges from overseeing internal security to running cricket affairs and occasional diplomatic troubleshooting. What makes him so powerful is that he answers to neither the prime minister nor parliament. His new assignment, however, looks exceptionally challenging. The proposed ‘administrative restructuring’ plan — its contours still unclear — has generated a political maelstrom that threatens the existing political order.

It has not only divided the federal cabinet but also ruptured the ruling alliance. The PPP has already launched a campaign against any attempt to divide Sindh under the pretext of administrative restructuring. A strongly worded resolution against the plan, passed by the Sindh Assembly last week, offers some insight into the volatility of the situation in the country’s second-largest province. The brewing conflict between the province and the federal government has now exploded, threatening to bring down the present political set-up. The rupture is hard to mend.

More intriguing, however, is the response of the prime minister and the ruling PML-N on the proposed administrative restructuring — said to be floated by the establishment. While there is no word from the PM, the differing voices from the PML-N and other cabinet ministers on the proposed plan presented by the interior minister make the entire issue extremely complicated. It is a house divided on a proposed plan whose framework remains obscure.

No move to restructure governance should be separated from the democratic process.

There seems to be complete confusion in the ranks of the ruling party. While some PML-N cabinet members and party officials appear supportive of the administrative restructuring, the party’s top leadership has maintained a conspicuous silence over the proposed plan. A big question also hangs over whether the PML-N leadership is prepared to support a plan to divide Punjab — its main power base.

Matters are getting murkier, with the establishment appearing adamant to go ahead with its plan with or without political support, as Naqvi has warned. With its governments in Islamabad and Lahore fully dependent on the establishment’s support for survival, the PML-N has no choice but to toe the line.

As for the PTI — the main opposition party, arguably the most popular in the country, which also governs the troubled province of KP — it may not oppose administrative restructuring on principle, but it will not support any imposed plan. With its mandate stolen and its leaders imprisoned, one cannot expect the party to accept any proposal that would strengthen the establishment’s control.

In this scenario, it will be extremely hard for the establishment to push through a plan requiring a two-thirds majority in both parliament and the provincial assemblies, as the Constitution demands. Even a constitutional amendment would need a two-thirds majority in both Houses, and with the PPP refusing to come on board, things could get messier.

Yet it seems the powers that be are not willing to back down. Their only choice, then, would be to go for a referendum, as Naqvi has hinted. With the PML-N and other coalition partners on board, it may not be difficult to get a referendum resolution passed by parliament with a simple majority.

Pakistan has a history of referendums being used by military dictators in an attempt to legitimise their unconstitutional rule. Who can forget the infamous referendum held by Gen Ziaul Haq to perpetuate his illegitimate government? Interestingly, the question was not whether Zia should stay as president, but whether voters would like an Islamic system to be established — a ‘yes’ vote was to count as validation of Ziaul Haq as president. Ballot boxes were stuffed to cover up the thin turnout, and the mockery further exposed the illegitimacy of military rule.

Gen Pervez Musharraf held a similar referendum to legitimise his rule, though there it directly asked voters to approve his presidency. While turnout remained low, the official statement declared massive support for the military ruler. Will the present dispensation resort to the same kind of fraudulent exercise to carry out its so-called restructuring plan? There is also a strong apprehension that a referendum could be used to enshrine a constitutional role for the security establishment in the power structure — a recent bill passed by parliament has only reinforced that speculation.

There are no two views that the country needs major restructuring to improve governance, but it cannot be separated from the democratic process. In a situation where the legitimacy of the entire system is questionable, no measure, however feasible it may sound, can be acceptable. Indeed, devolution to the lower tier of local government is essential if the system is to deliver, but in the absence of democracy, any administrative restructuring would likely strengthen authoritarian rule. No referendum can confer legitimacy on an imposed administrative structure. The proposal, though still unclear, has already polarised the country, and any referendum will only intensify chaos and instability.

The best thing for the country is to hold free and fair elections and let an elected parliament decide on the critical issues of administrative restructuring and devolution of power to local governments. The present establishment-backed rule, with its questionable mandate, cannot be expected to bring democracy to the grassroots. The lessons of the past must not be forgotten — of authoritarian regimes that tried to strengthen their control in the name of reform. A reminder to the interior minister who referred to Zohran Mamdani and Sadiq Khan: the two mayors are the products of democracy, and no leader like them can emerge under semi-authoritarian rule.

The writer is an author and journalist.

title: GSP+ concerns
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S preferential trade access to the European Union could be at risk. Brussels has cautioned that Islamabad can no longer assume continued trade concessions from the bloc. The warning comes at a critical moment in trade ties between the two. The current GSP+ scheme expires at the end of this year, with Pakistan seeking to enter into a successor arrangement — that has tougher conditions. The EU ambassador’s view that the outcome is “not certain” highlights a problem that extends beyond immediate negotiations. To preserve preferential access to its largest export market, Islamabad must prove it can meet the commitments it made under the programme. As the ambassador put it, “GSP+ preferences cannot be taken for granted”. Such unusually blunt language from a diplomat is significant, particularly for a trade arrangement worth more than €7bn a year to Pakistani exporters.

The GSP+ issue is also a test of whether Pakistan is prepared to honour its international commitments. The economy has benefited enormously from preferential access to the European market since 2014. That dependence makes Brussels’ latest warning especially serious. The European Commission’s 2023-25 assessment has found regression in several areas. It noted that improvements in legislation had not translated sufficiently into implementation. Its concerns included enforced disappearances, curbs on free expression, weak judicial independence and forced labour. Islamabad’s contention that the assessment lacks balance does not address these concerns. The successor scheme raises the bar, expanding coverage from 27 to 32 conventions. Pakistan has ratified the five additional conventions. But that is only a formal requirement. Brussels is now looking more closely at whether Islamabad is implementing them and wants evidence. Disputing Brussels’ findings cannot compensate for shortcomings in implementation when the successor framework explicitly places greater weight on enforcement. Hence, Islamabad faces the tough challenge of securing entry into the new framework. To do so, it must ensure that the deficiencies identified in the assessment do not put the EU’s existing preferences at risk during the transition. Treating the matter as diplomatic disagreement would be short-sighted. The issue is one of credibility, and Islamabad must show, through concrete actions, that its international commitments are more than promises on paper.

title: Joint tourism push
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE federal government’s plan to assume responsibility for seven roads spanning 464km across Gilgit-Baltistan is a welcome step towards improving access to one of Pakistan’s greatest tourism assets. The routes connect major destinations including Astore, Deosai, Skardu, Khaplu, Shigar and Naltar, and their rehabilitation and maintenance by the National Highway Authority could address a persistent weakness in GB’s tourism economy: unreliable connectivity. Landslides, flash floods, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods frequently sever road links, stranding visitors and residents alike and disrupting travel plans. Better roads backed by federal funding can therefore do more than shorten journeys; they can make travel safer, more predictable and more attractive to tourists. Reliable access can also encourage longer stays and repeat visits. The proposed toll on visitors may also be reasonable if locals are exempt and the proceeds are transparently used for road upkeep and related infrastructure.

However, roads alone will not unlock GB’s tourism potential. The centre and the GB government should use this initiative as the basis for a broader, coordinated strategy covering resilient infrastructure, emergency response, telecommunications, sanitation, waste management and reliable information on weather and road conditions. Tourist growth must also be managed carefully to protect GB’s fragile mountain environment. Local hotel owners, transporters, guides and small businesses should be involved in planning so that tourism generates livelihoods for communities rather than merely adding congestion and environmental pressure. Islamabad can provide resources and national-level infrastructure capacity, while the GB administration brings local understanding of regional needs. The two should also work together to promote lesser-known destinations, easing pressure on established tourist centres. Coordinated investment, regulation and promotion can make GB a safer, more accessible and sustainable destination.

title: Protest politics
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
WITH the PTI determined to march on the capital on Sept 27, a legal challenge to the planned protest has been lodged in the Islamabad High Court. The petitioner — ostensibly an Islamabad trader — fears disruption of routine life and business activities because of the protest.

While hearing the petition on Tuesday, the IHC formed a larger bench to hear the “sensitive” case, with the next hearing scheduled for tomorrow. Clearly, there is unease within the corridors of power regarding the PTI’s planned power show, which the party says is being organised for the “supremacy of the Constitution” and to demand the release of its founder Imran Khan.

The government’s concern was on full display in Karachi on Sunday, when large parts of the city’s road network were shut down on the day KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi was due to hold a rally at the Quaid’s mausoleum. Though the Sindh authorities claimed the shutdowns had nothing to do with the PTI’s planned activities and were carried out due to ‘security’ reasons, major thoroughfares had been blocked off on the day Mr Khan’s party was to stage its rally in the city.

The state believes that letting the PTI go ahead with the Islamabad rally could result in violence. These apprehensions are not without basis. After all, the November 2024 protest in the capital resulted in a deadly showdown between the party and the state. Yet there are two distinct issues that must be kept in mind.

Firstly, holding a protest is a democratic right, and the authorities should not be placing unnecessary obstacles in the PTI’s way. If the government blocks every democratic avenue to express grievances, it risks radicalising the affected parties. Secondly, though protest is a fundamental right, it must not turn violent. Attacks on law enforcers and harassment of ordinary citizens are unacceptable, and it is the responsibility of party leaders to ensure that their cadres remain non-violent.

It is not just the PTI that has sought to highlight its grievances on the streets; the Jamaat-i-Islami has been holding nationwide sit-ins over fuel prices for several weeks. While one may or may not agree with the reasons why these parties have hit the streets, their right to hold peaceful protest is undeniable.

When there are so many challenges confronting the people — high prices, economic volatility, terrorism, political uncertainty, erosion of democratic space, etc. — they cannot be expected to keep quiet, and have every right to voice their concerns publicly. The state should engage the PTI just as it engaged the JI to ensure that any protest is kept peaceful. The animosity should not be allowed to snowball into a fresh confrontation as the nation can ill afford more instability.

title: Sugar trap
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
ONCE again, the government is preparing to repeat an experiment that has cost consumers dearly. The sugar industry claims a surplus of 1.03m tonnes and wants immediate export permission. The government should resist until it has independently verified that figure. It cannot let the industry set both numbers and policy. There is good reason for scepticism. The Sugar Inquiry Commission documented export subsidies, alleged supply manipulation, underreporting and heavy windfall profits. The Competition Commission found evidence of price fixing among millers and later imposed penalties. Neither inquiry produced convictions or structural reforms, and the same mills accused of manipulation are setting the surplus number the government is being asked to accept. The latest episode is instructive. The government authorised roughly 750,000 tonnes of exports after declaring domestic supplies sufficient last year. Retail prices soon crossed Rs180 per kilo, and authorities had to arrange imports. The state pockets export earnings when supplies look plentiful, spending those on imports, and makes consumers absorb the cost when calculations are wrong.

This cannot happen again. Officials must independently reconcile production, stocks, consumption, exports, next year’s expected output and grower payments at the mill level before authorising shipments. A mishandled surplus could depress cane prices and hurt farmers. An overstated one could trigger shortages, inflation and another costly round of imports. The government must guard against both, without letting the sugar lobby dictate outcomes. That requires a transparent, rules-based framework: export volumes tied to a well-defined domestic reserve, with automatic restrictions once supplies fall below that level or prices rise sharply. Stock data should be verified by an independent body, and reconciliation figures published before export permission is given. Such a system would cut political discretion and make manipulation harder to sustain. The recurring sugar crisis is a governance failure. Successive governments have bent to industry pressure instead of building rules that can withstand it. The government keeps subsidising millers only to spend scarce foreign exchange importing sugar months later, privatising the gains and socialising the losses. The question is not whether Pakistan can export another million tonnes of sugar. It is whether the state can prevent the same commodity from being exported cheaply today and imported expensively tomorrow.

Published in Dawn, September 8th, 2026

title: Redrawing the map
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
IT has been quite something to watch a whisper become, in a matter of weeks, the state’s new “number one priority”. The trigger was the interior minister’s surprising admission at the Pakistan Economic Summit in late July that the present system had “collapsed”, and that new provinces and administrative reform were therefore urgently needed.

The political earthquake was immediate. For the PPP, already fuming over the AJK election, it was an insult added to injury. The president’s abrupt departure for London has since fed a good deal of speculation. Some believe that he went to press his allies in government to drop the idea altogether. Others have pointed out that his exit echoes another, years ago, when the PPP was being asked to make choices it considered political suicide. What can be said with certainty, however, is that an impasse has been reached.

The president had met the interior minister in London. Their interaction was recorded and shown in the media. It does not seem to have gone fruitfully. On his return, the minister doubled down on the need for new administrative units. The PPP answered with a Sindh Assembly resolution rejecting new provinces, and with speeches declaring “no compromise” on the province’s geographical unity.

The Sindh Assembly resolution deserves much more attention than it received given the implications for the drive for more provinces. Under Article 239(4) of the Constitution, the limits of a province cannot be altered unless the amendment is first passed by that province’s own assembly by a two-thirds majority. Sindh seems to have made its position plain by, at least symbolically, vetoing the proposal before it arrived at its door.

Before the country is dragged through another ugly crisis, those pushing for new provinces must explain how they intend to clear the bar set by the Constitution. They should also share what the new assemblies, secretariats and offices will cost, and where the money is to come from when citizens’ own pockets are already empty. There is no question that Pakistan needs better administrative management, but the stated end of restructuring — ie, better service delivery at the grassroots — is already provided for in Article 140A, and could be achieved far more cheaply by reviving, resourcing and actually holding elections for local governments.

Here, the political parties also share blame. They have spent decades hollowing out the LG system and alienating the citizenry. Any party that is unwilling to empower even a district council should not be arguing that the province is the only unit that matters. Therefore, though the LG system remains a less politically toxic option, it will only be considered an option if the political parties themselves make a renewed commitment to it. This is something they, too, must understand.

title: Resource curse
author: none@none.com (Dr Raashid Wali Janjua)
content:
AFGHANISTAN is becoming a classic case of the resource curse. Riven with factional fighting and reliant on a conflict economy, the theories of the resource curse are highly applicable to Afghanistan, presenting a gloomy prognosis of its economic and political future.

Despite the much-touted claims of $1 trillion in untapped mineral potential, Afghanistan has failed to realise that potential due to internecine conflict amongst various factions. On the one hand, there is a major division between the northern factions and the Interim Afghan Government, better known as the Afghan Taliban. On the other, there is an intense rivalry within the IAG between the Kandahari faction led by Mullah Hibatullah Akhundzada and the Haqqani faction based in Kabul. There are rich mineral deposits in the north and east of Afghanistan where Tajiks, Uzbeks and Hazaras mostly live. These groups resent any extraction of natural resources on their lands through IAG-sponsored projects.

The case of the Aynak copper mine offers interesting insights into the non-viability of the project. Problems include increased cost due to underground versus open-pit mining, lack of water for on-site smelting, high logistics cost for transportation of minerals away from the site, high cost of local power generation, and contentious royalty issues. The security cost due to attacks on Chinese workers has also been a dampener for investors. Deep down, the issue of internal jousting for control and royalty between the Kandahari and Haqqani factions is a major obstacle.

If a country lacks strong political institutions and a sound industrial base, and is not well integrated into the world economy, its susceptibility to the resource curse is a given. If Afghanistan starts mineral exports without functional banking and economic institutions, it runs the risk of contracting ‘Dutch disease’, in which inflation and the consequent high cost of imports nullify the export advantages, besides discouraging investments in non-resource sectors. Another downside of the resource economy is the risk of encouraging authoritarianism.

Infighting prevents Afghanistan from realising its mineral potential.

The worst impact of the resource curse is the prolongation of internal conflicts due to the ability of criminal gangs and militant factions to earn rents through resource exports and to use those for the continuance of conflict.

There are terrorist groups in Afghanistan, such as IS-K, Al Qaeda, ETIM, IMU and TTP, that are part of the internal and external conflict dynamics of the country. If these terrorist entities are in an ‘entente cordiale’ with the IAG, then they are also likely to stake a claim to Afghanistan’s mineral resources and use the income to consolidate their hold over the illicit Afghan economy. The internal conflict mosaic of Afghanistan also makes the actualisation of mineral resources extremely difficult as involvement in the extraction business by foreign companies might attract international censure along the lines of UNSC Resolution 1173.

The real fight over $1tr in mineral reser­ves is presently between the Kandahari and Haqqani factions of the IAG. Both are competing not only in a military capacity but also in resource mobilisation, as a result of which the mineral-rich provinces, largely inhabited by non-Pakhtun communities, bear the environmental, social and economic costs while deriving limited benefit from resource extraction. Major mineral resources are found in Hazarajat (Bamiyan, Daykundi — copper, coal), the north (Badakhshan — gems, lapis; Balkh/Sar-e Pol — gas, coal), and the east (Nangarhar, Logar — copper, gems, jade).

Though political power lies with the Kandahari faction, it was the business-savvy Haqqani faction based in the east that, after 2021, controlled customs, ports and the passport directorate, through which a huge share of state revenue flows. The Kandahari faction is now pushing back against that control by moving Haqqani-aligned officials out of customs and ports, replacing them with its own loyalists to wrest control of the most lucrative revenue stream in the country.

The tense stand-off between the two factions continues as Kandahar deploys troops in Badakhshan to assert the central government’s authority while the Haqqanis still manage to divert mining revenue away from mining sites in the east. As for the people, they lose either way. Mining under this system has promoted child labour, environmental destruction, and forced displacement of proximate communities. The extraction happens on their land, the profits leave the province, and neither faction is accountable to them.

Poor governance, non-existent institutions, terrorism, and a conflict economy have ensured that Afghanistan’s mineral resources have become a resource curse for that country.

title: Anti-drone division
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE ongoing wave of terrorism in the country has resulted in an unacceptably high number of casualties amongst security men, both police officers and military personnel. Despite the courage of security men, terrorists have often exacted a heavy human toll by adapting and altering their tactics on the battlefield. But now, a new unit launched by KP Police seems to be turning the tide by using technology to trace and neutralise terrorists before they can strike. The Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Division has been successful in lowering the threat level. Terrorist groups had been using drones, specifically quadcopters, to monitor security personnel and drop explosives. Police officials say that terrorist groups had seized modern equipment left behind by exiting Nato forces in Afghanistan, while hostile foreign actors were also said to be providing drone technology to violent elements. While the law enforcers had used anti-drone systems previously, a dedicated unit has had a visible effect on reducing terrorist attacks, and keeping tabs on terrorists in KP’s affected areas.

Police forces in other provinces, particularly Balochistan, which also suffers from a terrorist insurgency, should consider deploying similar units. For long, experts have said that police forces, which are on the front line of the battle against terrorists, must be given the requisite equipment and training to fight violent groups, and stay one step ahead of them. The UAV Division is one example of how the state can deploy the latest technological advances to quell the militant threat, and prevent casualties within the security forces by pre-empting the terrorists. As the KP police chief told this paper, there is “no other option … but technological advancement” to defeat terrorism. When terrorists use the latest technology, the state cannot expect to have the upper hand by using equipment and tactics that are decades-old, and suited to a very different battlespace.

title: International law prevails
author: none@none.com (Ahmer Bilal Soofi)
content:
IN its recent press release on ‘The Indus Waters Western Rivers Arbitration (Pakistan vs India), PCA Case No. 2023-01’, the Permanent Court of Arbitration has delivered an award in favour of Pakistan. The award, issued on Aug 31, 2026, strongly vindicates Pakistan’s position, which it has consistently maintained in diplomatic forums and in the international media. It illustrates that the principles of international law firmly support Pakistan’s case. Established in 1899, The Hague-based PCA is one of the world’s oldest institutions for the peaceful resolution of international disputes. It has earned considerable international standing for the integrity of its proceedings, the quality of its decisions and the calibre of the jurists who serve on its tribunals. It shares its premises with the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

Those who authored this verdict — the details of which will be made public soon — were selected under the procedure prescribed in Annexure G (Court of Arbitration) to the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), which requires arbitrators to be well versed in international law. Accordingly, the PCA is chaired by Prof Sean D. Murphy (US), a prominent international law scholar and practitioner. He sits alongside Prof Wouter Buytaert (Belgium), a specialist in hydrology and water resources; Prof Jeffrey P. Minear (US), an experienced legal practitioner; Judge Awn Shawkat Al-Khasawneh (Jordan), a former ICJ judge; and Dr Donald Blackmore (Australia), an expert in water-resource management and policy.

Pakistan had initiated proceedings, saying, “Look, the continued construction of two Indian hydropower projects violates the engineering requirements laid down in Annexes D and E of the IWT”. These requirements had been designed to ensure that water flowing to the lower riparian was not obstructed by engineering deviations in upstream projects. The concern, therefore, was that the construction by India, the upper riparian, in territory it controversially controls and occupies, could interfere with the flow of water intended to continue downstream to Pakistan. India had sidestepped this allegation by controverting the jurisdiction of the PCA and maintaining that the matter should only be brought before a neutral expert under Annexure F as it concerns “technical differences” rather than a “legal dispute”. Notwithstanding these objections, the court continued the hearing regarding the controversial hydroelectric projects.

The Permanent Court of Arbitration’s award in favour of Pakistan vindicates this country’s position.

Then on April 23, 2025, following the Pahalgam attack, India announced that the IWT would henceforth be held in abeyance. At this juncture, the PCA, seeking to satisfy itself that it possessed the requisite jurisdiction, invited both parties to make submissions. India, however, again chose to stay away. In contrast, Pakistan has always opted to participate in strategic litigation of this nature. In both the Kulbhushan Jadhav and Republic of the Marshall Islands cases before the ICJ, Pakistan overcame its initial hesitation. It chose to participate in the proceedings — a consequential decision that ensured its legal position was represented and defended before the court. The reasoning for this rests on an age-old law: if a party wishes to challenge a court’s jurisdiction, it must appear before that very court and object.

Even though Indian officials unleashed venom against the PCA and its proceedings, the court’s procedural wheels continued to turn. Eventually, it gave the present award, which destroyed New Delhi’s political basis for holding the IWT in abeyance.

The court approached the matter with considerable care. Rather than treating India’s refusal to participate as an opportunity to proceed on Pakistan’s case alone, it independently examined the legal arguments and factual circumstances that might have supported India’s position on placing the IWT in abeyance. The court went so far as to consider material available in the public domain, including statements by Indian officials explaining the reasons advanced for India’s decision.

The PCA then turned to the possible legal grounds on which India might seek to justify placing the treaty in abeyance. It examined whether the circumstances surrounding the IWT had fundamentally changed since 1960, taking into account demographic shifts, India’s growing demand for clean energy, advances in dam technology, and the effects of climate change. None, in the court’s view, met the demanding threshold required under international law to justify suspending or terminating a treaty. The PCA also considered India’s allegation that Pakistan’s frequent invocation of the dispute-resolution process constituted a material breach. Here too, the argument did not hold, and India could not establish a material breach on these grounds. The court held that this type of treaty couldn’t be treated as suspended even during armed conflict. Most importantly, it found that the IWT was intact and remained binding on both sides.

Allegations of cross-border terrorism against Pakistan have long occupied a prominent place in India’s political discourse. India expressly relied upon it in its April 2025 communication placing the IWT in abeyance, and alleging that Pakistan’s support for terrorism had undermined the basis on which the IWT could continue to operate. The PCA press release states that the court took this allegation extremely seriously, yet came to the conclusion that the act of terrorism was extraneous to the IWT and did not pertain to the treaty framework. The PCA went on to say that even if terrorism allegations against Pakistan were true, they would not be valid grounds for breaching the IWT. This was a very significant finding from Pakistan’s perspective, and it exposed the absurdity of Indian arguments against Pakistan, based on the latter’s unproved responsibility for the acts of terrorism.

The court’s interim measures effectively halt further construction and concreting by India while the neutral expert continues his examination of technical issues. Until that process is completed, India is expected to stop any work that could prejudice the proceedings or alter the position on the ground. We can discuss the consequences of any failure to comply — as well as the wider implications of the ruling — once the detailed award is released.

After the PCA’s verdict, the legal position is very clear: if you try to bring in political issues or issues extraneous to the IWT — which is a technical treaty — and such objections are taken up by any objective forum, defeat will be the writing on the wall — and that is what has happened with the Indian side.

The writer is a former caretaker law minister.

Published in Dawn, September 7th, 2026

title: A new dark age?
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
RECENT years have seen a surge of books and articles on the impact of technology on people’s lives and thinking. While communication technology has opened new vistas and opportunities it has also created its own problems in our digital age. Some works celebrate its benefits. Others warn of its damaging consequences especially those of social media. James Marriott’s The New Dark Ages: The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society joins this debate from another angle. The British journalist’s work falls within the genre that emphasises the harmful consequences of digital technology.

The book’s principal concern is that people aren’t reading anymore and that a screen culture is displacing a print culture. For Marriott, the spread of literacy and the kind of thinking nurtured by the world of print drove progress in economic development, scientific advancement, and the emergence of modern democracy. In a print culture, he argues, knowledge is organised, understood, and contextualised. “Books make arguments, propose theses and develop ideas.” This process, he contends, develops the power of reasoning.

For Marriott, this is getting lost in an era where the smartphone has taken over our lives and become the main reason for the decline of reading. There has never been a technology quite like the smartphone, which has so much distracting content that it keeps people’s attention endlessly on the screen. He maintains that a hostile environment for learning has been created by this digital distraction. Screens are changing human behaviour. Smartphones are shaping a “fragmented, trivialised and angry new world”, in which conspiracy theories and mad ideas are spread at terrifying speed. The spread of knowledge is impeded by this and is actually breaking down. Political discourse once grounded in logical argument now takes place “amid the moronic inferno of social media”.

Marriot attributes much of the 21st century’s disorder and unreason to the fading of the written word and the “colonisation of culture” by addictive screens. He sees the intellectual hollowing of society as a consequence of the decline of reading and the world becoming a less rational place. Public discourse today, he claims, has become trivial to the point of dysfunction. It has affected politics too as this environment encourages the rise of mediocre politicians with little understanding of history, whose appeals to the public are emotional and do not rest on rational propositions. Politics, Marriott argues, is growing “angrier, stupider and more obsessed with personality”. He laments the fact that the full ramifications of the onset of what he calls a post-literate society are not fully understood.

Marriot may be overstating his case and exaggerating the damaging impact of digital technology. But he is no outlier in this assessment. Last year in a compelling book Superbloom: How Technologies of Connection Tear Us Apart, Nicholas Carr surveyed how digital technology — including smartphones, the internet, social media and artificial intelligence — is transforming both people and societies. He argued that instead of broadening minds, expanding empathy and fostering harmony, this technology has had the opposite effect. It is eroding understanding and trust and contributing to strife and social disharmony.

Communication technology offers immense opportunities but has serious unintended consequences.

For Carr, speed and intensity in the flow of information and stimuli compel people to rely on intuitive thinking based on biases. It deprives them of the ability to tap into deeper analysis. As a result, it has undermined reasoned analysis, methodical evaluation and contemplative inquiry. As he puts it “Attention splinters, understanding grows thin”. This results in mental shortcuts and shallow thinking. Thus “rather than levelling barriers to knowledge, it becomes a barrier itself”.

For both Marriott and Carr, the information spread through digital vehicles does not foster knowledge but detracts from it. “More informed does not mean better informed.” The fragmented nature of information provided by the screen makes much of it useless, according to Marriott. Social media further dumbs down the public conversation. Marriott sees social media and short-form videos producing junk content and misleading posts. He also finds a connection between video platforms like TikTok and increased vote share for populist and far right parties. That’s because feeds by such parties play on emotions and abjure reasoning.

Carr’s book devotes far more attention to social media. His criticism is unsparing. He also takes tech companies to task. In his view, social media amplifies falsehoods and hostility rather than promote facts and truth. Because it is shorn of communication barriers, it brings out people’s worst instincts. He also blames the “ugly content that pervades the social media” on tech companies and on algorithms. As he puts it, “Social media churns out information that’s been highly processed to stimulate not just engagement but also dependency.” By encouraging excessive and unchecked self-exposure to a mass audience, it shatters all boundaries. The result is discord, not harmony.

An earlier book also warned of a world of fractured attention. In The Lonely Century, economist Noreena Hertz had a different focus, but she also addressed the harmful effects of communication technology and social media. She assigned a central role to social media and smartphones in making people “more angry and tribal”. Drawing on research, she argued that technology and social media were also fuelling a global loneliness crisis, both personal and political. Smartphones “fragment our attention”, estrange us from people and “create a splintered self”. Hertz saw social media trapping people into isolated digital bubbles and creating a meaner, more aggressive world. This is evident in trolling and other forms of online abuse. As a result, she urged the acknowledgement of the dangers of “tech addiction” and making social media platforms accountable.

Communication technology has brought immense benefits to society. At the same time, it has involved serious unintended consequences. Where there is promise there is also peril. Managing the negative effects of new technologies remains a difficult challenge without easy solutions. With artificial intelligence the risk is even greater as it is growing much faster than our ability to control it.

The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.

title: Online danger
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE digital age contains death traps for children. A new Unicef report reveals a global child exploitation emergency. About 20m internet-using children across 21 countries, including Pakistan, faced online sexual exploitation in a single year; 60pc of reported violations were on digital platforms while 14pc occurred in online gaming. More than one in five children became targets of sexual exploitation; 15m were exposed to sexual images, and 4m had sexual material “shared without permission”. Almost 1.1m reported AI-generated sexual images or videos showing them. Sadly, these numbers are just the tip of the iceberg. Online predators follow a perversion pyramid. Offences begin with chatting and sharing of inappropriate content then assume the form of solicitation, ‘sextortion’, and misuse of AI deepfake technology.

These statistics mean permanently damaged lives. The scale of the crisis is a consequence of keeping the scourge hidden. Victims of tech-facilitated sexual violations are reportedly four times more vulnerable to self-harm, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts. As abusers are often known to the victims, voicing these traumas is difficult for reasons of shame and ostracisation. Whether it happens online or offline, the toll of abuse is lifelong. It impedes education, employment and productivity. To keep children from harm, protections to ensure a safe digital space are crucial. Legislation must possess commitment, transparency and precision; enforcement lapses should be punishable. As in the West, there is a need for Pakistan to restrict social media use for under-16-year-olds. But the onus of digital safety lies with the parents. No law can succeed until the authorities and society stop slinking around this grave issue. Totally darkened screens can hamper learning and information. Instead, investment in police training, a cyber-patrol force to track down web criminals, and active encouragement to report dangerous online spaces are vital. While an evolving cyberspace is hard to secure, it cannot be allowed to cripple the young.

Effective solutions require robust legislative frameworks with commitment and transparency, parental responsibility in digital safety, and state investment in police training, cyber-patrol forces, and public awareness campaigns to report online dangers.

title: Climate test
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE world is edging into climate territory governments have spent years trying to avoid. A new UN Environment Programme report warns that the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming threshold is likely to be breached within the next few years. That does not mean climate action has failed or that the target no longer matters.

UNEP argues that humanity must keep any “overshoot” as low and brief as possible, as every fraction of warming raises the risk of extreme weather, ecosystem loss and irreversible tipping points.

Adding to the concern, the World Meteorological Organisation says the El Niño strengthening in the Pacific could be the strongest in four decades, intensifying heat, drought and floods worldwide. For Pakistan, the fallout could include water stress, food insecurity and greater strain on urban infrastructure and services.

The Nepal-China floods have shown how quickly climate hazards can devastate lives. As warming intensifies, Pakistan will increasingly have to contend with several climate stresses at once, often in places least equipped to cope. That demands a rethink of how the country plans for development.

Pakistan must plan for a climate changing faster than its institutions. Adaptation cannot remain confined to emergency response after floods, heatwaves or droughts. Development policy itself must change.

New housing, roads, power systems and urban drainage should be built for harsher weather. Water policy must account for uncertain river flows and rainfall. Agriculture needs crops and irrigation methods better suited to greater heat and water stress, along with support to help farmers adapt. Cities require heat-action plans, shaded public spaces and stronger protection for outdoor workers.

A World Bank assessment covering Pakistan and the wider MENAAP region found that prolonged extreme heat is depressing sales, labour productivity and wages, showing that climate damage is also an economic competitiveness problem. None of this absolves the major emitters. UNEP identifies finance, equity and global cooperation as essential to navigating a dangerous climate future, while stressing that countries with greater responsibility for global warming must act fastest.

Pakistan should press that case. But it must also spend development resources intelligently. The age of treating climate disasters as one-off emergencies has ended and it must plan for a harsher reality.

Climate damage is an economic competitiveness problem, requiring Pakistan to invest development resources intelligently and press major emitters for global cooperation and finance.

title: The fertility option
author: none@none.com (Kulsoom Hisam)
content:
WHY does a woman have to know today whether she will want to become a mother tomorrow? Some women want children, some are unsure, and some may never want them at all. In Pakistan, where the biological clock is often accompanied by reminders of shaadi ki umar and warnings of future regret, egg freezing remains an uncomfortable idea.

Recently, US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez documented her egg-freezing procedure on social media. While many praised her openness, others criticised her for delaying motherhood. The discomfort is likely to be even greater in Pakistan, where marriage and motherhood remain deeply intertwined. A recent Dawn feature, ‘How to freeze your eggs in Pakistan’, shows that the procedure is available in Pakistan, alongside stigma and practical barriers. Rather than treating fertility-preserving technology as something to fear, we should ask what problem it is trying to solve. Several economic ideas help explain why freezing one’s eggs can be a rational response to uncertainty, without implying that every woman should do it, or even that every woman ultimately wants children.

‘Real options theory’, developed prominently by Avinash Dixit and Robert Pindyck in Investment Under Uncertainty (1994), shows that when decisions are difficult to reverse and the future is uncertain, keeping an option open can have value. Egg freezing offers a similar option: a woman may later use her frozen eggs, never need them, or decide she does not want children at all. Its value lies in preserving the possibility of motherhood without requiring her to decide today what her future self must want.

But the value of keeping an option open depends on what time allows. This is where ‘search theory’ becomes useful. Marriage is a search problem: no one knows when a suitable partner will appear, while waiting can bring both benefits and costs. In Pakistan, those costs are also shaped by the marriage market. Recent research by Bashir and Nazir (2025) highlights the importance of family networks, finding that nearly half of marriages are consanguineous, most commonly between first cousins. Waiting is therefore not simply a private calculation between a woman and her biological clock; it occurs within family networks and social expectations. For a woman who wants children, declining fertility can make continued search costly. Egg freezing cannot remove the uncertainty of finding the right partner, but it may reduce one cost of waiting and give some women greater freedom to reject a match that does not feel right.

The value of keeping an option open depends on what time allows.

But uncertainty does not end with finding a partner. A woman may also be uncertain whether motherhood will remain part of the life she wants. Economics allows for heterogeneous preferences: one woman may be certain she wants children, another may want to preserve the possibility, and another may decide motherhood is not for her. These are different preferences under uncertainty, not different degrees of rationality.

This matters because women are often asked to make reproductive decisions through the language of future regret: ‘what if you change your mind?’ Graham Loomes and Robert Sugden’s ‘regret theory’ shows how anticipated regret can shape choices under uncertainty. Applied to reproductive decisions, regret can run in multiple directions. A woman may regret not freezing her eggs, but she may also regret paying for a procedure she never uses; she may regret not having children, but she may also regret becoming a parent under pressure. The question is not how to eliminate regret, but which risks a person is willing to bear.

Yet regret is not formed in a social vacuum. ‘Identity economics’, assoc­iated with Geo­rge Akerlof and Ra­­c­h­­el Kranton, arg­u­­es that choi­ces are shaped by social identities and the norms attached to them. In Pakistan, marriage and mo­­therhood are treated as expected stages of a woman’s life. Slamat, Bracke and Ceuterick (2026), studying childless women in rural Punjab, describe motherhood as socially obligatory and find that women are expected to demonstrate mothering qualities and seek treatment to validate their desire for motherhood. In such a setting, even anticipated regret may be shaped by social expectations.

Egg freezing is valuable precisely because it can give women more room to make personal decisions on their own timeline, though that freedom will remain unequal as long as access is limited by cost. Finding the right partner is difficult, and not every woman who wants children will meet that person in time. Some will freeze their eggs and later use them; others may decide motherhood is not the life they want. Reproductive freedom should mean having space to pursue motherhood, postpone it, remain uncertain about it, or reject it altogether.

The writer is an assistant professor of economics at St Olaf College.

title: Nourishing Pakistan
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S nutrition crisis is not short of diagnosis. What it lacks is the machinery and political discipline to act on what is known. That was the most useful message to emerge from DawnMedia’s two-day Act for Nutrition conference in Islamabad, where experts argued that malnutrition cannot be confined to the health sector. Over four in 10 children under five are stunted, while the economic cost of malnutrition is estimated at $17bn annually. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal’s promise that the Planning Commission will take ownership of nutrition and early childhood development is therefore significant. It recognises that this is a human-capital and development crisis involving health, agriculture, education, water, sanitation, population policy and social protection.

Speakers also stressed that 30pc to 40pc of stunting occurs before birth, making maternal nutrition, antenatal care, birth spacing and the first 1,000 days of life critical. Adolescence, too, cannot remain the forgotten interval between childhood and motherhood. Equally important was the emphasis on water and sanitation. Feeding a child better will achieve little if contaminated water and repeated infection undermine growth. Calls for targeted WASH investment in high-burden districts should be taken seriously. The problem is that Pakistan has heard much of this before. Policies exist, programmes operate and donor money flows, yet nutrition remains fragmented among institutions that rarely plan, finance or deliver together. The Benazir Nashonuma Programme shows that progress is possible. Children enrolled in it were found to be 22pc less likely to be stunted at six months. The challenge is to connect such interventions with primary healthcare, family planning, clean water, sanitation and local social services, rather than treating each as a separate scheme.

The conference’s proposal to regard nutrition spending as capital investment rather than simply health expenditure is also worth pursuing. Preventing stunting is investment in future learning, productivity and national income. But declarations must now give way to measurable commitments. Pakistan still relies on the 2018 National Nutrition Survey for its headline 40.2pc stunting figure, an extraordinary data gap for a crisis repeatedly described as a national emergency. A fresh national survey, dedicated budget lines, provincial and district targets, named officials responsible for delivery and regular public reporting should be the minimum next steps. Recognising food and nutritional security as a basic right may strengthen the framework, but rights without budgets and accountability remain promises on paper. Pakistan knows how malnutrition comes about and what can reduce it. The failure is no longer one of knowledge. It is the state’s failure to organise itself around the child. The conference has sharpened the diagnosis. Government must now prove it can deliver.

title: How many more?
author: none@none.com (Rida Hosain)
content:
IN Pakistan, violence against women and girls is a human rights crisis. Hina Zareef was reportedly killed by her father for leaving an abusive and forced marriage. In another horrifying case, a woman was reportedly burned by her in-laws during a quarrel. Hina Javed was brutally murdered in her marital home.

The reality is that, for many, a woman who asserts her autonomy is seen as someone who must be punished. Hina Zareef’s case was categorised by many as an ‘honour’-related crime. There is no honour in violence and control. Honour belongs to the woman, who had the immense courage to walk away from abuse, only to be killed by her own family.

There have been several recent reports of violence against minor girls. A minor girl in Abbottabad was reportedly sexually assaulted at school, while the autopsy of a five-year-old from Haripur has revealed that she was raped. The rot in our society is deep. It is high time we recognise the scale and seriousness of the violence being inflicted and confront it with urgency.

There must be an honest acknowledgement of rape culture in our society. Rape culture is reflected in the attitudes that justify violence, and the immediate instinct to question the victim. It is reflected in a society where we place great emphasis on controlling girls while failing to place the same emphasis on how boys are raised. It is sustained by the silence of other men who witness abusive behaviour but do not challenge it. It is reinforced by the drama industry that continues to portray controlling behaviour as romance and glamourises violence.

For many, women asserting their autonomy must be punished.

Many have advocated for the importance of sex education and conversations about consent as essential tools in challenging rape culture. It is crucial to teach children about bodily autonomy and the meaning of consent. That they have a right to say no and, equally, that they must respect another person’s no. When such conversations are treated as taboo, ignorance and harmful stereotypes take over.

Despite passing anti-rape legislation, domestic violence laws, and amendments addressing ‘honour’ crimes, a severe gap exists between enactment and implementation. This is reflected in the dismal conviction rates in cases of gender-based violence. There is a lack of political will, and a judicial process that in many cases involves re-victimisation. Last year, the Lahore High Court held that where a valid marital bond continued to exist between a husband and wife, the husband could not be prosecuted for rape.

Under the Hudood Ordinance, zina-bil-jabr (rape) was defined to exclude acts between individuals who were validly married. Subsequently, the Protection of Women (Criminal Laws Amendment) Act, 2006, introduced a revised definition of rape, and the marital rape exception was removed. Presently, the law no longer includes an exception for marital rape. If the legislature removed marriage as a barrier to a rape prosecution, the courts must not resurrect that exception. The most disturbing part of the ruling is it effectively treats marital status as a shield against allegations of sexual violence.

In ‘Hassan Ahmed vs the State’, which is before the Supreme Court, the trial court and the high court convicted the accused for rape. The Supreme Court converted the conviction for rape into fornication. The Punjab government filed a review against this decision which was dismissed.

As matters stand, the judiciary in Pakistan accepts that a case involving an alleged rape can be converted into fornication (even though fornication was not included as one of the offences in the charge). The court did not simply find the evidence insufficient to su­­stain a conviction for rape. It imputed consent and effectively treated the failure to establish rape as proof of consensual sexual intercourse. There is a fundamental differen­­ce between finding that there was insufficient evidence, and im­­plying consent where the complainant has expressly stated that she did not consent.

The Supreme Court went on to say that “the complainant is also liable to be proceeded against and punished as an accused of the offence of illicit intercourse with consent”. A woman who comes forward to report sexual violence should not have to fear that, if the prosecution fails to prove rape to the required standard, she herself may be put in the dock. In a society where fear, stigma and social consequences already silence countless victims, the risk of women being put on trial will only deepen that silence.

Regrettably, dangerous stereotypes continue to persist in our jurisprudence: that the existence of a domestic or intimate relationship diminishes the allegations of violence, and that consent may be inferred from the circumstances rather than established as an express and voluntary choice.

At every level, we are failing the victims.

Despite progressive anti-rape legislation, domestic violence laws, and amendments addressing 'honour' crimes, a significant gap exists between law enactment and effective implementation, exacerbated by a lack of political will and judicial processes that often lead to re-victimization.

Recent judicial rulings by the Lahore High Court and the Supreme Court have undermined legislative efforts to protect women, specifically by reintroducing a marital rape exception and converting rape convictions into fornication, effectively implying consent where none was given and creating fear among victims.

Dangerous stereotypes persist in Pakistani jurisprudence, where domestic relationships diminish allegations of violence, and consent is inferred from circumstances rather than established as an express, voluntary choice, leading to systemic failures in protecting victims and perpetuating impunity.

title: Bond revival
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN has raised a record $3bn in its single largest international capital market transaction through a dual-tranche Eurobond sale that drew nearly $6bn in total orders.

When international investors offer to lend a country almost twice what it is asking for and are willing to do so for as long as 10 years, they are betting that Pakistan will still be solvent, still servicing its debt, and still worth holding paper on a decade from now. That bet placed by a widespread group of institutional buyers gives yet another positive spin to the economic revival story told by the government.

Two years after the country was on the verge of default, that is no mean achievement. Some practical gains from this stand out: a boost to reserves, a fresh pricing benchmark, and less reliance on bilateral rollovers. Locking in money for 5.5 and 10 years, rather than the shorter rollovers that have dominated Pakistan’s external financing in recent years, pushes out the point at which this debt has to be refinanced. Following recent rating upgrades, this is the kind of market validation the country needed.

None of that should be mistaken for cheap money, though. The coupon rates — almost equal to returns the government is paying on Roshan Digital deposits — are real, high rates in a hard currency Pakistan cannot print and is struggling to earn. For context, when Islamabad last issued dollar bonds in 2021, it borrowed five-year money at 5.875pc and 10-year money at 7.375pc. In other words, this deal costs more than the last comparable one did. Part of that gap can be attributed to international factors: global dollar rates have stayed higher for longer since the Fed’s tightening cycle, so every sovereign borrower, not just Pakistan, is paying more than it would have three or four years ago.

But part of it is also Pakistan-specific. Investors are still charging a risk premium that an investment-grade country would not pay. That does not mean Pakistan has borrowed badly. It is just that the current ratings can only do so much in the prevailing market.

Comparing Eurobond coupons across countries can be tricky because a rate that looks high for one issuer can be a bargain for another, once credit rating, tenor and the global rate environment are accounted for. Judged against peers of similar credit standing, Pakistan’s pricing sits towards the upper end of the range, which aligns with where the rating agencies currently place it: not investment grade, but no longer treated as a basket case either.

The more useful test of this deal will come later: whether Pakistan can return to the market in a year or two and borrow at a lower cost than it did with this issue will be the real test. It will determine if the confidence on display is durable.

title: Searching for past glory
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Amir Rana)
content:
THE collective memory of Muslim societies, particularly in the West and South Asia, is based on the persistent idea that since the collapse of the Ottoman Empire they have been in need of a joint response to challenges ranging from politics to defence. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia may be seen as something of a pioneer on this front with the creation of the Islamic Military Alliance to Fight Terrorism in 2015, which was partly the basis for the recently concluded Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. However, Pakistan has always championed such ambitions. The roots go much further back, with the Baghdad Pact representing an important milestone in that journey.

The concept of a collective Muslim response has been conceived and framed in different ways, from the idea of the ummah to its more structured institutional expression within the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Its character has continued to evolve as changing political objectives have redirected the ideological orientation of Muslim states. In Pakistan’s case, however, this idea has shaped not only the country’s ideology but also its internal politics and models of state structure.

There is little doubt that Pakistan’s growing role in the Gulf, beginning with Trump’s Gaza peace plan, followed by the Islamabad MoU and now the Makkah accord, has boosted the country’s confidence. However, when its leadership looks inward at the political and economic conditions, the contrast undermines some of the confidence gained from its successes in an evolving geopolitical environment. This disparity frustrates the power elite, that wants to address internal problems immediately and sustain the country’s momentum in the external arena.

To achieve internal stability and order comparable to that in Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, Pakistan’s other regional partners, the power elite here appears prepared to take several political risks. These could include major administrative engineering, such as the creation of new provinces, a step that would come at considerable political cost.

Pakistan is deepening its West Asian ties to bolster its defence power and strategic weight.

This argument is not intended to evaluate the costs and benefits of creating new provinces. Rather, it seeks to trace the trigger that makes the power elite nervous when its external successes do not correspond with domestic political realities and the state of the economy. There can be several interpretations of this contradiction, ranging from the political economy to the changing geopolitical order. Yet an important dimension is often missing from the debate: the triangle of ideology, statecraft and geography.

Pakistan and Turkiye share a geographical anxiety: their military power and ambitions do not fully correspond with the territories they control, while their opportunities for geographical expansion are extremely limited. This creates a middle-power anxiety about sustaining and enhancing their military and defence capabilities.

Both countries are responding to this challenge in their own ways. Turkiye is pursuing regional groupings, alliances and transnational Turkic partnerships. Pakistan, meanwhile, appears to be abandoning its old strategy of ‘strategic depth’ or the attempt to expand its influence to neighbouring territories to overcome its geographical anxieties. Instead, it is engaging more deeply in West Asia to strengthen its defence capabilities and strategic weight. The purpose is obvious: Pakistan faces a much larger geographical and military power in India.

Saudi Arabia faces a different middle-power dilemma. Its primary concerns are sustaining economic stability and protecting itself from regional forces that it perceives as ideologically hostile or hegemonically ambitious, principally Iran and Israel. Saudi Arabia has learned to coexist with Israel, but Israel’s hegemonic ambitions continue to generate anxiety about the future regional order. Riyadh is also concerned about hostile forces near its borders, particularly in Yemen, where Iran has effectively projected its influence.

Pakistan is now going a step further by undergoing a state-centric ideological recalibration. This transformation does not yet match Saudi-style social liberalisation or the secular-nationalist transformation associated with Nasser’s Egypt. Pakistan is still struggling to find a clear direction. Its emerging model appears to combine Mohammed bin Salman’s state-controlled “moderate Islam”, the mutually reinforcing nationalism, military authority and state-regulated religious discourse of Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s Egypt, and Turkiye’s religious-conservative identity, nationalism and defence-industrial ambition.

Briefly, the power elite wants religion to remain under state authority. It seeks a transition from transnational Islamic solidarity to the national interest; the creation of a modern, technologically capable Muslim state; religious scholars who support national cohesion rather than challenge statecraft or the ambitions of the ruling elite; and centralised control over security and foreign policy.

However, the power elite also believes that the existing political order, governance model and constitutional arrangements obstruct the achievement of lasting stability. Interestingly, the Afghan Taliban, once close allies of Pakistan’s establishment, have taught it an important lesson: Islamist allies may possess their own nationalism, interests and territorial ambitions, which may not correspond with the vision of another country’s power elite.

Middle powers with complicated neighbourhoods and significant defence capabilities often have additional strategic thoughts. They imagine renewed glory through alliances with friendly states possessing compatible capabilities and ambition. Major powers frequently exploit this tendency by encouraging middle powers to form alliances.

Washington is encouraging the emerging defence architecture that has taken shape through the Makkah accord. China and Iran, meanwhile, are waiting for the US to reduce its regional footprint before revealing or advancing their own designs.

The US and UK exploited this middle-power tendency several times during the Cold War. The Baghdad Pact was the most developed form of such an alliance. Established in the mid-1950s, it brought together Turkiye, Pakistan, Iraq, Iran and the UK. However, the project eventually collapsed due to internal upheavals in Iraq and Iran, and Turkiye also experienced domestic political instability.

At that time, Pakistan was considered the alliance’s most stable regional partner, with politics largely under control and an economy that appeared to be flourishing. Pakistan’s power elite still dreams of returning to those days of perceived glory and reclaiming the country’s position among the leading middle powers of the Muslim world.

The writer is a security analyst.

title: Shame and shamelessness
author: none@none.com (Salahuddin Ahmed)
content:
“You must never lose your sense of shame. If one is past all shame, what is one fit for? One lives like a bird in moult, shedding virtues like plumes all pointing down to hell” — Wolfram von Eschenbach (German poet.)

I’VE been wrestling with this idea — the essentiality of shame for retaining humanity — for some time now. But I am reminded of it every time I read in the news about how one judge or the other has, again, successfully continued Imaan Mazari and Hadi Chattha’s perverse incarceration.

The novel Shame presents another take on the idea. While acknowledging its necessity, it argues shame is never truly lost. It is suppressed, it is unacknowledged, it is transferred to others, but it invariably re-emerges, nay erupts, mutated into manifestations of violence and tyranny throughout society.

Surviving in Pakistan (but, more specifically, thriving in Pakistan) demands the suppression of shame. Being more fortunate, we suppress the shame of a cruel and rapacious system built to profit the powerful by exploiting the powerless. As Muslims, we suppress our shame at how we steadily criminalise the very existence of our minorities and force them to leap through ever-higher hoops to earn their right to live. As citizens, we suppress the shame of a state that has long abandoned any pretence to being representative and casually disappears dissidents. As lawyers, we suppress the shame of a legal system indifferent to justice and riddled with cowardice and venality. We suppress the shame, not only from fear of the consequences of speaking or acting, but so we can live with ourselves.

There are a few, however, who feel the sting of shame more sharply. They speak, and act, while we watch. They carry the burden of our collective shame and expiate it.

There are a few who carry the burden of our collective shame and expiate it.

Imaan and Hadi belong on that list. One might not subscribe to all their opinions. One might think them misguided in some of the causes they choose to advocate. And, while ensconced in the quiet safety of one’s living room, one can disagree with their or, more particularly, her manner of articulation. But while we may not possess the courage to emulate them, do we lack even the shame to admire them?

This January, Judge Afzal Manjoka sentenced the couple to prison for 17 years. As per the judgement, Imaan’s crime was sending six tweets. In one, she posted a picture of Mahrang Baloch raising a victory sign and encouraged the public to raise their voice against fake encounters, enforced disappearances and killings in Balochistan. In another, she said innocents kept in illegal detention and torture cells were also victims — just like those targeted in terrorist attacks. In a third tweet, she said state repression in Balochistan was making the insurgency worse. In a fourth, she argued that reports about anti-terrorist operations by security officials in Balochistan had lost credibility.

Two of her tweets were about KP. In the first, she said “we said never forget but acted like nothing happened. The terrorist who had our children slaughtered was set free by the state. The disastrous good Taliban vs bad Taliban policy continues even today”. Presumably, she was referring to the TTP’s former spokesperson, Ehsanullah Ehsan, who initially surrendered and was detained in a military safe-house but later ‘escaped’ and claimed to be living the expatriate’s dream in Turkiye. Notably, the parents of the 147 children in the Army Public School massacre earlier raised the same grievance in their petition before the Supreme Court. Her second tweet condemned the forced disappearance of Ghazi Amanullah, brother of PTM leader Manzoor Pashteen, and argued the state was targeting peaceful dissidents and their families.

As I said earlier, one might object to the tenor of some of her speech. But the content? Who seriously disagrees that the good Taliban, bad Taliban strategy we’ve followed on and off in Afghanistan and Pakistan for three decades has, on each occasion, come back to bite us? Or that decades of the state’s undiscriminating repression in Balochistan has only fuelled the insurgency? But even if you disagree, and are a genuine adherent of the ‘Pindi knows best’ philosophy, do you reckon people expressing the contrary view should be convicted of terrorism and jailed for 17 years?

Poor Hadi, of course, didn’t even tweet anything himself. The judgement accuses him, however, of retweeting four of Imaan’s tweets. Unstated in the judgement (but imprudently expressed by Chief Justice Sarfaraz Dogar in an earlier, unrelated, case) is his true crime: being a Pakistani man who cannot control his own wife.

But my question is not to Judge Manjoka, nor about how closely his judgement of Jan 24 hews to the narrative expressed in the press conference held on Jan 6 by a security official accusing Imaan of being “a lawyer for terrorists” and “a foreign agent”.

My question is to everyone who wears a judicial robe: how is it possible to witness the travesty of Imaan and Hadi’s trial, the breach of every principle of due process, the utter frivolity of the charges against them, the draconian punishments awarded to them, and not feel an outpouring of shame at one’s own helplessness?

It is to everyone who wears a black coat. How can one belong to a profession committed to upholding the rule of law yet observe the presidents of the Supreme Court Bar and Islamabad High Court Bar (belonging to the Asma Jahangir group, no less!) defending these convictions; and witness the failure of the majority of bars to rise to the defence of their own, without feeling the sharp sting of shame?

The question is about the nature of shame itself. What happens to a society forced to live without it?

The writer is a member of the Pakistan Bar Council.
