title: Meltdown in PCB
author: none@none.com (Saad Shafqat)
content:
ANYONE who has even casually followed Pakistan cricket over the years will know that our cricket board’s response to losing the current Test series in England is a hysterical overreaction. After consecutive defeats at Headingley and Lord’s sealed the fate of the three-match rubber, the Pakistan Cricket Board sacked the head coach and fast-bowling coach, ordered seven players from the squad to pack their bags, and announced five novices and two recalls as their replacements. On top of that, one of the openers will be subjected to a disciplinary investigation for allegedly faking an injury.

As actions of the PCB administration go, this is unprecedented. As human behaviour goes, this is lunacy.

These developments have unleashed a deafening outrage, triggering embarrassing news headlines and sarcastic social media memes. That Pakistan’s cricket establishment has degenerated into such farce should come as no surprise. The PCB chairman has always been a handpicked political appointee — merit be damned. And since a fish rots from the head, there you have it. Yes, sometimes you will get lucky with the arrival of a Nur Khan or an Arif Abbasi at the helm, but these are fortuitous exceptions.

A national cricket board chief is meant to be an elected official, voted in by representatives of regional cricket associations. This makes the position approachable and accountable. Instead, the practice in Pakistan is for the prime minister to dole out the PCB chairmanship as a favour or reward to an ally or acolyte.

The typical outcome is whimsical and incom­­petent governance. Over time, this has resulted in a cricketing infrastructure that lacks the ability to identify, nurture and promote the best talent available.

As actions of the PCB administration go, this is unprecedented. As human behaviour goes, this is lunacy.

The one silver lining in this whole fiasco is that the ire of the cricket-following public has finally been deflected away from the players and squarely onto the PCB and its leadership. This is as it should be. We would normally have the players in our gunsights, as they are the most visible and hence the most obvious targets. But the blame ultimately lies elsewhere.

To shine on the international stage, a cricketing tradition must rest on three pillars — an avid fan base, a rich talent pool, and a capable administration. There’s no question about the avidity of the fan base, nor about the richness of the talent pool. Just look at the whiplash that Pakistan’s cricket supporters go through with every victory and every defeat; that tells you all you need to know about their passionate commitment. As for talent, a country that has managed to produce all-time legends such as Javed Miandad, Zaheer Abbas, Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis and Younis Khan (among many others), is certainly not lacking in cricketing ability. That leaves governance and management, by far the most compromised pillar in Pakistan’s cricket edifice.

It is honestly very hard to fathom what deliberations would have taken place in the upper echelons of the PCB that led to such a ridiculous knee-jerk outcome. It couldn’t have come from the high-performance director Aqib Javed, the lone international cricketer in PCB’s C-suite, because he would surely know better. Quite possibly Aqib mi­­ght have advocated for a more measured appro­ach. Yes, he has been staunchly defending the PCB’s actions in the media and on public forums, but the PCB command structure leaves him little choice.

In all likelihood, the decision-making came solely from the PCB chief, Mr Mohsin Naqvi, himself. He may have asked for input from other bigwigs in the PCB’s corporate hierarchy, but none of them have any serious cricketing credentials. One can easily imagine them trying to guess what the boss wanted to hear, and then echoing it implicitly and explicitly.

What thought process did Mohsin Naqvi undertake to do what he did? By the looks of it, not a very rigorous one. He is, to begin with, an overburdened man, holding the portfolio of federal minister for interior and narcotics control, in addition to his PCB hat. Moreover, he has emerged as a key member of the diplomatic team seeking peace in the Middle East, having visited Iran no less than six times since hostilities started. This mandate amounts to averting ‘World War III’, no small assignment. So we can reasonably conclude that Mr Naqvi as a cricket administrator is at best distracted, and at worst negligent.

Meanwhile, there is still the issue of the cricket itself. Pakistan are scattered and scarred after losing the first two Tests. One can only imagine the terrified mood in the camp as the team anticipates the third and final Test, starting in Birmingham on Sept 9. Cricket is a funny game and a turnaround in Pakistani fortunes is theoretically possible, but the odds are of course heavily against it. The team is weak and demoralised, if not outright traumatised. Cricket fans have been left wondering if this is the worst Pakistani cricket outfit ever.

It is worth remembering, however, that Pakistan cricket has seen much worse, both on and off the field. In 2002, in what is easily our worst Test scorecard ever, Pakistan faced Australia in a Test in Sharjah, totaling 59 in the first innings and 53 in the second, losing (naturally) by an innings — even though that team had included some great names. Then, in 2009, there was the terrorist attack outside Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium that nearly killed the visiting Sri Lankan side. And in 2010 we had the spot-fixing disaster, which ended two highly promising fast-bowling careers and sent three Pakistani cricketers to London’s Crown Court, and thence to prison.

Thankfully, we are now far removed from those catastrophes. The challenge ahead is to improve on-field performance and restore our international competitiveness. It won’t happen overnight, but if we can somehow manage to sort out the Gordian knot that is the Pakistan Cricket Board, that would make for an appropriate start to a revival of lost glory.

The writer, a professor of neurology at Aga Khan University, has written on cricket for international publications.

title: Fires, symptoms & the disease
author: none@none.com (Zafar Mirza)
content:
Accidents are nurtured over years; they don’t happen just like that — Qabil Ajmeri

MY last column on these pages was titled ‘Collapse and consequences’. I borrowed ‘collapse’ from the interior minister and added the consequences myself, illustrating the latter with the fast-unfolding HIV epidemic in Pakistan. The epidemic has infected at least 7,500 innocent children; they contracted the virus through unsafe medical care at our health facilities.

Today, when I sat down to write this column, another horrible consequence of collapse is before me — 14 newborns died in the fire at the Mother and Child Health Ward of the largest public sector hospital in Islamabad. One columnist has called it murder, and rightly so.

Indeed, the catastrophe on August 26 has sent shockwaves through the system and society. When and how it leads to a seismic shift is yet to be seen. Most people are not very hopeful. They believe that the incident will gradually fade away. Other shocking headlines will replace it in the media and public memory. But I disagree. Being a chronic optimist, the only option I have is hope. The system will change. It has to change. There is no other option.

The fire and the deaths nevertheless are the symptoms of an underlying disease which has spread across the health system. Let’s talk about children’s deaths in the country from a public health perspective.

The system will change. It has to change. There is no other option.

The neonatal mortality rate (NMR) is defined as deaths of newborn children within 28 days after their birth per one thousand live births. This rate is a function of many factors: the health of the mother (49 per cent of women of reproductive age suffer from iron deficiency or anaemia); the birthing place, meaning deliveries taking place at home at the hands of untrained birth attendants (31pc of births in Pakistan are still attended by untrained birth attendants) or by a trained midwife. After birth, 80pc of deaths take place due to prematurity; birth asphyxia and sepsis, which are neonatal infections. All of these are almost entirely preventable causes. Each day, 691 newly born infants die in Pakistan before they complete the first month of their life due to the conditions in which they arrive in this world and how they are handled on their arrival. In a year, 248,500 children die before the age of 28 days in Pakistan.

Let’s bring a perspective to it. Pakistan has the world’s third largest and Asia’s highest neonatal mortality rate. Yes, you read it right. In Pakistan, more children die per 1,000 live births before 28 days than any other country in the world except South Sudan and Nigeria. Our NMR, according to 2024 UN IGME data, is 36.1/1,000, for South Sudan it is 39.5/1,000 and Nigeria 39/1,000. Two countries below us are also sub-Saharan African countries: Somalia 34.2/1,000 and Zimbabwe 33.7/1,000. We have a higher NMR than Afghanistan, India and Bangladesh. In Iran, this rate stands at 7.2. In Sri Lanka it is 6.6. The NMR can be as low as one or less. For example, it is 0.9 in Japan, 1.1 in Singapore, 1.4 in Sweden, 2.6 in China and UK and 3.6 in USA.

A deeper analysis of the exceptionally high NMR in Pakistan shows that there are remarkable differences in the deaths between the rich and the poor, and between provinces. The national figure of NMR of 36.1/1,000 is actually 51/1,000 among the poorest in the country; 85.2pc of rich mothers are assisted by skilled birth attendants whereas only around 30pc of poor mothers have the same facility. Punjab has the highest NMR among all the provinces in Pakistan ie 51/1,000 and within Punjab, the NMR in the district of Chiniot is 65, while in Lahore it is 35.

What this tells us is that we are amongst the worst in taking care of our newborn children. The fact that Asia’s highest NMR is in Pakistan reflects the dismal state of our healthcare system and socioeconomic conditions, especially for the poor. We are among the lowest spenders on health and we spend it very inefficiently. Our primary healthcare is very weak. Our public healthcare system is plagued with a governance crisis that has resulted in an ongoing and deepening public health crisis in the country. The NMR is just one symptom.

So, the tragic loss of 14 newborns at Pims is actually the eruption of a volcano that has been churning for a long while. This is not the first eruption, and unfortunately this may not be the last either. Dawn has listed 31 hospital fire incidents across Pakistan since 2010. It is a non-exhaustive list.

A keen reader of this column may be itching to ask me: why are you still optimistic? The reason is rather simple: I have no other option but to be so. We have to fix this system, and it can be fixed. Let me share an example.

There were only three hospitals in Pakistan until November 2024 which were accredited by the Joint Commission International (JCI). JCI is a stringent and prestigious international benchmark of quality and patient safety. The three hospitals included AKU, SKMH and Shifa International. All of these are in the private sector. In 2024, Pakistan Kidney and Liver Institute and Research Centre (PKLI&RC) also got JCI accreditation. PKLI&RC is a public sector hospital and it has become the first government hospital not just in Pakistan but in South Asia to have achieved this honour. It has an independent board of directors and it makes its own decisions. The government supports it through public money but does not interfere in its functioning. PKLI&RC now has filter clinics in 18 districts of Pakistan accredited by JCI, proving that it is possible to deliver at the primary healthcare level. This is a great model to learn from. I hope that by learning from this model and the MTI experience, the public sector hospitals can be structurally reformed soon.

But the real underlying public health crisis of which NMR is just one indicator looms large. And a much greater intervention is needed here. This is also possible. The history of the National Health Service in the UK and what role the Beveridge and Black reports have played in its development and strengthening contain so many lessons for us, only if we are ready to wake up and develop a will to reform.

The writer is a former health minister, adjunct professor of health systems and president of Pakistan Association of Lifestyle Medicine.

The dismal state of healthcare is attributed to inefficient health spending, weak primary healthcare, and a profound governance crisis leading to an ongoing public health emergency.

title: Chiniot dam plan
author: none@none.com (Naseer Memon)
content:
ARE Sindh and Punjab set to enter into a round of hydro tensions? This time, a string of dams on the Chenab river are being proposed. The case for one of the four — the Chiniot dam — has been presented to Irsa by Wapda. The Chiniot dam is envisioned as a multi-purpose project on the Chenab, about 100 kilometres downstream of the Qadirabad barrage and 5km from Chiniot city. According to the project’s PC-1, the reservoir will have a gross storage capacity of 1 MAF. The project envisages the storage of surplus monsoon flows, flood mitigation, the generation of 80MW of hydropower, and water supply to Faisalabad city. The structure includes an earth-fill main dam, two gated barrages, 77km of reservoir dykes on both banks, and a surface powerhouse.

Wapda, through this initiative, is quietly reviving the Cholistan project, which the Council of Common Interests halted last year. The project is riddled with serious flaws. In a technical appraisal, the federal planning ministry has made more than 50 observations regarding the project. A working paper reveals that the project will inundate about 47,000 acres of land within the floodplain of the Chenab river; the local population is deeply concerned about the loss of their agricultural land, livelihoods and residential structures.

The estimated cost of the project is Rs298 billion, of which the federal government will finance 80 per cent. Wapda will serve as the executing agency. A technical appraisal has also questioned the cost and time rationale. Wapda’s dam portfolio of Bhasha, Dasu, Neelum-Jhelum and Nai Gaj dams has been plagued by years of delays and cost overruns of several billion rupees. Wapda failed to complete any of these projects within the allocated cost and time framework.

Intriguingly, Wapda has submitted the PC-1 to the pre-Central Development Working Party meeting, without an approved environmental impact assessment. This undermines the EIA’s significance, reducing it to a mere formality. Stakeholder consultation is a critical component of the EIA. But the PC-1 is silent on whether the lower riparian, Sindh, was consulted as a highly important and vulnerable stakeholder. Wapda’s presentation before Irsa shows four dams on the Chenab at Wazirabad, Mudh Ranjha, Chiniot, and Shah Jewna, with a total storage capacity of about 4.5 MAF.

Sindh has expressed serious concerns about the dam.

Moreover, Wapda plans to increase the capacity of three upstream link canals. Recently, the Jalalpur canal was commissioned with an estimated annual withdrawal of 0.5 MAF. In the case of a project cascade, EIAs for individual projects are not advised. Instead, a strategic EIA is needed to understand the full spectrum of potential environmental and social impacts. Wapda should disclose all projects as a single package, as they will have a huge cumulative impact on the lower riparian.

Technical appraisal has also pointed to an inexplicable claim of an irrigation benefit of Rs35,768 million per year for claimed 80,000 acres. It works out to Rs447,000 per acre per year, which is four to nine times higher than the realistic agricultural revenue in Punjab. The federal ministry has said that the estimated economic internal rate of return of 18.67pc is based on implausibly inflated assumptions.

The appraisal has also raised concerns over possible dam failure in Pakistan’s third-largest city and an industrial hub downstream. It warns of an ominous scenario for a dam with storage capacity of 1 MAF behind 77km of dykes. Any dyke failure could prove catastrophic, especially as an emergency action plan is missing. During the 2025 floods, Che­nab attained a peak of 1,077,951 cusecs on Aug 27. It created a risk for the Qadirabad barrage, which has a capacity of 900,000 cusecs. The administration had to artificially breach the right marginal bund to secure the barrage structure.

Sindh has expressed serious concerns about the project. The building of the Chiniot dam will mark the start of the construction of several storage and diversion structures. The flow data of 1999-2025 reveals that Punjab’s barrages below the Rasool-Qadirabad-Sulemanki link canals received almost 16pc less than the allocated share of water in the early Kharif season. Water availability had plummeted to -36.4pc by early June. The PC-1 mentions that the filling of the Chiniot dam is to commence in June. The dam’s construction can place severe stress on downstream areas in Punjab, leading to excessive withdrawal of the Indus through link canals. The situation will be compounded when all four dams require storage. Sindh often remains water-stressed in June. Additional withdrawals will adversely affect flows of Sindh’s barrages.

The writer is a water governance expert.

title: New AJK government’s task
author: none@none.com (Ahmed Bilal Mehboob)
content:
DESPITE hurdles, doubts, speculation, a protest movement and delayed polls on seven out of 45 directly contested Legislative Assembly seats, the task of installing a new government in Azad Jammu and Kashmir has finally been accomplished. There had been serious questions about the fairness of the elections. The bitterest criticism was from the PPP, the PML-N’s ally in the national parliament.

Even the AJK prime minister’s election was not without controversy. Barrister Iftikhar Gillani was not selected or even recommended as a candidate for the office by the PML-N parliamentary party of the AJK assembly; rather, he was picked by the president of PML-N Pakistan. The choice was resented by some senior party leaders, including Shah Ghulam Qadir, the party president in AJK, who boycotted the assembly session that elected the PM.

The key objection to Mr Gillani’s election as PM was not his relative inexperience compared to veterans such as former PM Raja Farooq Haider or former speaker Shah Ghulam Qadir but the mode of his election as an assembly member. He had lost his seat — the Muzaffarabad constituency, LA-29 — to his PPP rival in the election by over 3,000 votes. Still, he returned to the assembly on a seat reserved for technocrats. There is no legal bar to the eligibility of a member who is defeated in the general election and subsequently elected on a reserved seat to seek the PM’s office. But many politicians believe that a PM should win the confidence of his constituency before seeking the coveted position.

However, despite a turbulent electoral phase that had been ongoing for some months, the new government and PM have assumed office in AJK. Given the PML-N’s clear majority in the assembly, the election of a new AJK president of the PML-N’s choice will likely be a formality. The most important question, however, concerns the new government’s agenda and how far it can overcome the most serious challenges ever faced by an AJK government.

A negotiated solution must be found for all contentious issues.

In view of the circumstances surrounding the entire electoral process, the foremost challenge before the new government and the PM is to establish the government’s moral and performance legitimacy, even if one accepts its electoral legitimacy. Opening the lines of communication with the outlawed Joint Awami Action Committee, engaging with the saner elements within the organisation, and convincing them to abandon the agitation will be the government’s first major test. If successful, it will pave the way for legitimacy of performance. Although the outlawed JAAC can justifiably be blamed for several irresponsible and anti-state utterances and actions, the fact remains that the defunct organisation has a sizeable following, especially in Poonch division, where, despite its best efforts, including organising phased polls, the AJK Election Commission could not hold elections in seven out of 11 constituencies.

A sizeable crowd has been staging a sit-in for almost three months, partly paralysing civic life and links with the rest of AJK and Pakistan. The confrontation and deaths of some agitators and law-enforcement personnel have polarised Kashmiris not only in AJK but also among the diaspora. This confrontation has damaged goodwill and the moral standing of authorities in AJK and Pakistan. The situation, therefore, must be defused immediately and a negotiated solution found for the contentious issues.

It was unreasonable, arguably, for the outlawed JAAC to insist on immediately abolishing the 12 AJK assembly seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees settled in various parts of Pakistan. This demand became even more absurd after the AJK Supreme Court ruled in June that the legislative assembly seats reserved for refugees were constitutionally protected and could not be abolished through executive action or street protests. However, it is also true that the constitutional reforms on the allocation of seats between refugees from the occupied Kashmir valley and Jammu need to be seriously considered, along with the election procedure. The election to the AJK assembly from various parts of Pakistan is generally heavily influenced by the federal and provincial governments during the poll cycle. Now that the new legislative assembly is in place, it should seriously initiate deliberations on constitutional reforms.

In general, the outlawed JAAC’s demands are not unreasonable and are mostly directed at welfare measures and better governance. For example, the demand for a smaller cabinet and the abolition of lavish facilities for elected representatives and senior bureaucrats should be sympathetically considered, alongside calls for roads, tunnels, bridges, safe drinking water, and preventing development budgetary funds from lapsing. Demanding empowered local governments and elected students’ unions is also fair. These are not just JAAC demands, but what every Kashmiri and also many in Pakistan demand. The new government can build on the previous government’s acceptance of most demands and begin implementing the points already agreed upon.

The new PM may begin by forming a smaller cabinet and cutting back on unnecessary protocol and unproductive spending. If tangible steps are taken early for better governance, a solid foundation may be laid for broader reconciliation. In the long term, both the federal government in Pakistan and the AJK government should consider granting AJK the same rights and privileges enjoyed by the four provinces. The same goes for Gilgit-Baltistan.

A constitutional way should be found to provide interim representation to AJK and GB in federal institutions such as parliament, the Council of Common Interests, the National Economic Council and the water regulator Irsa, without compromising our position on the Kashmir dispute. The denial of these rights over the last 80 years has become a major source of grievance.

The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.

title: Beyond listings
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S request to Unesco to consider Rani Ghat and Banbhore for the World Heritage List is welcome. It follows the recent expansion of the country’s tentative list from 25 to 37 properties, with 12 new cultural and heritage sites added this year.

Both Rani Ghat and Banbhore speak to civilisations that flourished on this land long before the modern state existed, and greater international recognition could help attract scholarship, tourism and conservation funding.

Plans to take Gandhara exhibitions abroad, establish “Gandhara Corners” and facilitate longer visits to Buddhist sites are also sensible. Pakistan has for too long treated its archaeological wealth as a niche interest rather than a cultural and economic asset. But enthusiasm for adding names to Unesco’s list must be matched by equal seriousness about the six Pakistani properties already inscribed on it.

Similar vigilance is required at Lahore Fort and Shalamar Gardens, where planning and development around the property must not compromise its heritage value.

The record there is mixed. The World Heritage Committee this year acknowledged conservation progress at Mohenjodaro and Makli, while making clear that considerable work remains. Mohenjodaro still requires attention to drainage, salinity and an integrated management plan; Makli needs sustained conservation and adequate financial and human resources.

Recognition cannot become an end in itself. Federal and provincial authorities should publish conservation plans and budgets for every listed site, maintain specialist teams, improve visitor facilities, signage and access, and promote these places intelligently and consistently at home and abroad.

Tourism revenues should be transparently reinvested in preservation, with local communities given a stake in protecting the sites. Seeking recognition for Rani Ghat and Banbhore is worthwhile.

But Pakistan’s strongest case for adding new treasures to the World Heritage List is to show that those already recognised by the world are being cared for as if they matter.

title: Ties with Kabul
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
WHILE diplomatic efforts are underway to restore dialogue with Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, as the Foreign Office has pointed out, talks can only succeed when there is a firm commitment from Kabul to end support for terrorist groups based on Afghan soil.

During a briefing on Wednesday, the FO welcomed China’s efforts to bridge the gap between Kabul and Islamabad, but cautioned that only firm action from the Taliban could take the process forward. Beijing’s envoy for Afghanistan was recently in Pakistan reportedly to restart the Urumqi process. The FO also downplayed the recent engagement of the Afghan ambassador to speak at the NDU as “not unusual”.

This may be true, but the fact that the Afghan diplomat spoke at the nation’s top defence university at a time when bilateral ties are near rock bottom is significant. But, despite these efforts, the fact remains that terrorist groups based in Afghanistan are the biggest obstacle to peace. The ISPR announced yesterday that several terrorists trying to infiltrate Pakistan at the Afghan border were eliminated. The military’s media wing highlighted that “the Afghan Taliban regime has consistently failed to ensure border management”.

The efforts by sincere friends like China are welcome. Beijing wants calm in the region to protect its investments in Afghanistan, as well as to neutralise anti-China militant groups such as ETIM based on Afghan soil. Yet, as the FO pointed out, these endeavours can only succeed when there is determination from Kabul to take action against terrorist groups. The Taliban regime has taken steps such as relocating TTP fighters and their families away from the common border, while the Taliban supreme leader has also reportedly asked the banned TTP to stop attacks on Pakistan. But these are cosmetic moves, and as the latest firefight at the border indicates, they have had a limited impact on the TTP and other terrorist groups.

If diplomatic efforts are to succeed, then the roadmap, as identified by the FO, must be followed. This entails “verifiable, written assurances” from the Afghan Taliban that their territory will not be used against Pakistan. If this apparently simple principle is followed, engagement and long-term peace are possible. It may be worth reviving the Urumqi process, but Kabul must affirm its resolve to act against anti-Pakistan terrorists.

While sustained hostilities are not good for either country, Pakistan has shown that it can defend itself against terrorist groups, as well as states that host them. Pakistan has said time and again that it is ready for dialogue if Afghanistan withdraws its support for violent groups. It is now up to Kabul to create a conducive atmosphere for talks, primarily by stopping all cross-border movement of terrorists.

Published in Dawn, September 4th, 2026

title: ‘Kindly adjust’
author: none@none.com (Ehsan Malik)
content:
‘KINDLY adjust’ is a peculiarly South Asian expression. It means tolerating inconvenience or accommodating what is not quite right. While courteous, it captures the relationship between citizens and the institutions that govern them. When electricity disappears, arrange a generator. When water is scarce or unsafe, call a tanker and install a filter. When schools, hospitals, roads or air disappoint, pay privately, reroute, stay indoors or stretch the household budget. In other words: kindly adjust.

Pakistanis have become exceptionally good at adjusting. What we proudly call resilience is often the ability of citizens to compensate privately for the failure of public institutions. Those with money buy electricity, water, education, healthcare, security and protection. The middle class stretches to follow; the poor endure or leave for work abroad.

But there are limits to adjustment. The recent deaths of newborn babies in a fire at Islamabad’s premier government hospital brought this home with unbearable force. When something as fundamental as the safety of infants in a public hospital cannot be assured, institutional failure is no longer an inconvenience. It becomes a matter of life and death.

Pakistan’s problem is that government too often mistakes programmes, budgets, authorities and committees for real delivery and measurable achievement. Education is counted in schools, teachers and budgets, not whether children learn. Healthcare is counted in hospitals and beds, not outcomes and safety. Environmental policy represents aspiration while citizens face unreliable supply, polluted air and untreated waste.

The first adjustment, therefore, must come from government itself. Public institutions should be judged by outcomes. Every major public service should publish standards: learning outcomes, hospital safety, healthcare availability, affordable and reliable utilities including safe municipal water and garbage collection. Performance against them should be public. When government fails, citizens pay through illness, lost productivity and private expenditure.

Resilience has become an excuse for poor governance.

Accountability must match authority. Pakistan has many officials empowered to approve, regulate, inspect and prohibit, but too few who are clearly answerable when things go wrong. Each disaster is followed by an inquiry, suspension or committee, yet real learning remains elusive. Serious failures should automatically trigger independent investigation. Regulators need professional leadership. Senior appointments should carry measurable objectives. Authority without consequence encourages indifference.

Government also needs capability. Car­eer civil servants remain indispensable, but a modern economy needs specialisation, lateral entry, merit-based appointments, fixed tenures and measurable objectives. The aim is to combine institutional experience with specialist knowledge and managerial competence. Government must also simplify procedures, reduce overlapping respo­nsibilities and give managers enough auth­ority to be accountable. Pakistan needs better people in government, and systems in which good people can perform.

The state must also reconsider what it tries to do. Pakistan has a government that is simultaneously too large and too weak: involved in too many activities, yet frequently unable to deliver basics. It should do fewer essential things much better at lower cost, which would also reduce the burden of taxes on the narrow formal sector.

Another adjustment is to take government closer to citizens. Pakistan dev­olved authority to the provinces under the 18th Amend­m­ent but largely fai­led to complete the journey. Neighb­ou­rh­ood water, garb­age collection, primary schools, local roads and district hospitals require empowered elected local governments with pred­ictable resources and clear accountability.

None of this absolves citizens or businesses of responsibility. Citizens cannot demand good services while evading taxes, stealing electricity, encroaching on public land, bribing officials or ignoring regulations. Businesses cannot demand predictable policy while seeking exemptions, protection and preferential treatment. Citizens should pay fair taxes and obey reasonable laws. Businesses should compete rather than seek privilege.

For too long we have treated people’s capacity to cope as a national virtue. But resilience has become an excuse for poor governance. As Pakistan approaches its 80th year, citizens should not be expected to continue to adjust to shortages, inflation, insecurity, poor services, weak regulation and repeated economic crises. The state must deliver through declared standards, competent management and strong accountability.The elite who can afford to bypass state services should join the masses in demanding delivery.

The writer is a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and of the Pakistan Business Council.

title: Jumping the gun
author: none@none.com (Nazir A. Jogezai)
content:
THE Balochistan government has announced that future government employment will be made possible through an AI-based recruitment system managed by a dedicated unit. This method, it claims, will be transparent and based on merit. There is a general consensus in society regarding the fact that public employment should be free from political pressures, opaque decision-making, and unnecessary delays. However, this step, despite the promise of strengthening meritocracy through technology, must be carried out with careful consideration.

We often witness initiatives in specific sectors, finance in particular, where technology filters in to replace manual and cash-based processes with digital payments, automated government systems, AI and data-driven tax administration, online public services, and a modern financial infrastructure. Their goal is to shape a more transparent and efficient form of governance. But the overall management of administrative nerve centres is largely conducted via paper files, handwritten approvals, and the physical movement of files from one office to another.

Administrative records remain fragmented, the workflow is slow, and routine processes almost entirely dependent on procedures designed decades ago.

Against this backdrop, AI-based recruitment appears as an isolated technological intervention — a digitised gateway to a largely unchanged, outdated and status quo-driven bureaucratic structure. Unfortunately, the pattern of isolated initiatives is particularly pronounced in public administration in underdeveloped countries. The pattern can easily be termed an ‘automation island’. While it can enhance individual functions, institutional restructuring of governance is compromised.

The greatest risk is not that AI makes mistakes but that humans stop questioning its conclusions.

Supporters of AI-based employment methods argue that algorithms can improve efficiency, reduce human bias, and strengthen merit-based hiring. Automated systems can process thousands of applications within minutes, apply standardised evaluation criteria, and minimise arbitrary interference. While these assumptions may hold true for the public sector, its practices are fundamentally different from those of the private sector. A democratic state pursues fairness, legality, accoun­tability, transparency, and public trust. Upholding these values through algorithms is no mean task.

Algorithms are biased; they alter the source of bias but do not eliminate it. A Stanford study analysed a dataset of four million applications through an AI-based screening tool. It found bias against African and Asian candidates, reflecting the assumptions embedded in the design, the quality of the training data, and the priorities of developers. AI can reproduce recruitment bias as it learns from past hiring patterns. For instance, if candidates from elite universities were hired often, an AI tool may rank such applicants higher. The primary flaw in AI-based recruitment systems is the ambiguous concept of responsibility, which in conventional recruitment rests with public officials. In contrast, no algorithm carries constitutional or legal responsibility.

The second flaw is the automation bias. Public administration researchers interpret this as the decision-makers’ tendency to accept computer-generated recommendations without critical scrutiny. The greatest risk is not that AI makes mistakes, but that humans gradually stop questioning its conclusions.

The establishment of a dedicated AI-based recruitment unit suggests that AI has been treated as a separate administrative function rather than another means to strengthen governance. The unit boasts financial and technical expertise with institutional support. Studies on public administration have consistently warned against creating new entities such as AI-driven recruitment systems. These duplicate existing responsibilities, create overlapping jurisdictions as well as increase administrative fragmentation instead of reducing it.

Governments integrate typewriters and computers as tools to assist operations. These are not treated as independent functions or as separate departments. Additionally, real transformation re­­­­quires combining the latest technology with org­anisational, legal and administrative alterations.

It would have been more appropriate had the government introduced digital governance — electronic file management, process re-engineering, integrated dashboards, cybersecurity, digital records, citizen services, and a responsible application of AI across governance functions. These steps will make recruitment one element of a comprehensive digital governance ecosystem with ample consideration for technological shortcomings, preventing a specific technology from being pitched as a justification for a new institutional structure.

The promised arrangement forces us to ask an uncomfortable question: what exactly are we recruiting for? At present, it seems that we are using AI to recruit more efficiently for yesterday’s bureaucracy. The technologically recruited personnel will continue with the same old administrative tasks — maintain records, retrieve files, draft routine correspondence, process applications, and manage documentation. Ironically, these are precisely the activities that AI assists or automates around the world. Sadly, an AI-assisted recruitment scheme will only help preserve a governance model that has become archaic — transporting files from one office to the other.

Historically, what has dominated the sequence of events in governance areas is the introduction of highly visible technologies to project a modern image. In AI-based recruitment, AI serves as a ‘technology of symbolism’ rather than a technology of management. AI undoubtedly carries significant appeal today. But we must not confuse technological sophistication with institutional reforms.

Purchasing and installing software is easier than redesigning bureaucracy. Such announcements are convenient and temporary replacements for improving our organisational culture. The objectives of transparency and merit in public recruitment are important. We must, therefore, appreciate the digital push by Balochistan’s authorities. But AI can boost recruitment efficiency; it cannot, on its own, overcome recruitment biases or modernise governance. The government must show a commitment to reforming institutions. The launch of new technologies in the same system is counterproductive. A digitised model risks prioritising technology over a long-overdue governance overhaul.

Published in Dawn, September 4th, 2026

A significant risk is 'automation bias,' where decision-makers uncritically accept AI-generated recommendations, thus shifting accountability from human officials who bear constitutional responsibility.

True governance reform requires comprehensive digital governance (electronic file management, process re-engineering, integrated dashboards, cybersecurity) and institutional overhaul, rather than just symbolic technological adoption.

title: Kashmir PM, CPEC and the crisis of credibility
author: Imtiaz Gul
content:
Four recent developments explain the credibility - or the absence of it - of Pakistan's self-centred, visionless rulers and the inability of the archaic, rent-seeking bureaucracy. Both remain anchored in a mindset that has resulted in squandered opportunities. These developments also highlight the contradictions and gaps between words and actions, ideals and practice. There is little doubt that the country is facing an acute crisis of credibility and integrity. Every delay in critically important plans, every constitutional or moral violation and every defiance of Supreme Court orders makes this crisis more serious.

Firstly, the selection of Azad Kashmir's Prime Minister on a technocrat seat is nothing but a brazen affront to the people at large. Voters had rejected Iftikhar Gillani in the general election, but Nawaz Sharif - on the face of it - dumped his long-time associate Shah Ghulam Qadir, only to undermine his own slogan: "Honour the vote." Why would the voter - betrayed in February 2024 - trust him or the system anymore?

Secondly, on August 30, the Central Development Working Party (CDWP) recommended reducing the estimated cost of the "Construction of Water Supply Scheme to Gwadar Town from Mirani Dam under Balochistan Socio-Economic Development Projects Phase-III" by around 20 per cent, to Rs23.82 billion, against the Rs29 billion proposed by the Balochistan government. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal directed the provincial government to initiate a study on wastewater treatment in Gwadar, observing that the city should not be allowed to become another Karachi, with sewage polluting the sea.

The forum, however, asked ECNEC to approve the project subject to satisfactory resolution of outstanding technical observations, particularly regarding demand figures, hydrology, confirmation of the water source, procurement strategy, land acquisition status, a self-sustainable operation and maintenance (O&M) strategy and a realistic implementation plan.

Staggering, isn't it? Eleven years after the signing of multiple CPEC projects, with Gwadar at the centre of it all?

Equally intriguing was another meeting on August 28, chaired by Ahsan Iqbal, which formally rejected a Frontier Works Organization (FWO) proposal for developing the 460km Rohri-Multan section of ML-1 and decided to explore alternatives for this section. The estimates did not adequately include locomotives, coaches and operating costs.

Isn't it telling that a minister who has been crying hoarse about CPEC being a game-changer, including the Gwadar and ML-1 projects, is now seeking alternative sources of funding? He nevertheless deserves commendation for two things: a) refusing to clear the FWO proposal for the Rohri-Multan section because of multiple deficiencies; and b) ordering an independent audit of the costing prepared by the organisation itself.

The August 28 meeting offered yet another sad comment: planners have not finalised the ML-1 proposal, let alone secured alternative sources of funding. Nor do they appear serious; reportedly, only junior officials represented the federal ministries involved. This suggests that the bureaucracy does not expect the project to take off anytime soon.

It is a sad story indeed. Until shortly before Covid-19 struck in late 2019, the Chinese leadership was more than keen to finance the entire ML-1.

"Brother, $78 billion are peanuts for us, but tell your people to come prepared with feasible plans on ML-1. We have also worked very hard to get here and expect others to follow the same path," a very senior Chinese official told me when I asked about the possibility of funding for ML-1.

What the meeting confirms is that Beijing's promised financing for the project is no longer forthcoming. For years, the promised investment was presented as the backbone of ML-1. Now the government is struggling to fill the gap.

But with its incompetence, the Pakistani bureaucracy - presumably including those with vested interests in the West and those disinclined towards Chinese investment and influence in the country - stalled the Chinese goodwill, and the project seems to have finally hit a dead end as far as Beijing is concerned.

It is perhaps a blessing in disguise that the Chinese stepped back from their earlier commitments on ML-1 financing. Why? Our politicians and bureaucracy have already messed up Chinese power-sector investments through spiralling circular debt, delayed loan repayments and hurdles in profit repatriation.

The larger issue relates to the rule of law. Locals and foreigners alike are shocked by the way superior court orders are flouted by the authorities. The latest reversal, on September 2, of a 2022 Islamabad High Court (IHC) judgment on naval farms and the sailing club offered yet another glimpse into the exceptionalism exercised by the higher courts when it comes to protecting deeply entrenched power elites. Of late, Supreme Court and IHC orders concerning former Prime Minister Imran Khan have been spurned more than once.

Such defiance of the rule of law hardly inspires confidence among the people at large or foreign investors. They see that if companies from even a "time-tested friendly country" such as China face enormous administrative and legal challenges, what could possibly happen to investors accustomed to having absolute confidence in the judiciary and the rule of law?

title: Managing external debt
author: none@none.com (Ishrat Husain)
content:
PAKISTAN’S debt has crossed Rs100 trillion raising doubts about the stabilisation programme’s veracity. First, it’s not advisable to use absolute amounts or per capita debt. The correct way is to use indicators that relate public debt stock and debt servicing to national income, exports of goods and services, revenues, total foreign exchange earnings and foreign exchange reserves to gauge the future capacity to discharge these obligations.

To begin with, clarify the various definitions that have created a lot of confusion in laymen’s minds. Pakistan’s total debt and liabilities consist of public debt and private debt. Public debt accounted for 91 per cent of the total stock of outstanding debt and liabilities on June 30, 2026. The remaining 9pc is the private debt mostly to borrowers abroad, for which the government has no fiscal obligation. However, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) has to provide foreign exchange to service this debt.

Within the gross public debt, the government’s share was almost 92pc while the balance was owed by public enterprises but guaranteed by the government. Borrowing from the IMF is also included in the gross public debt, although it is the SBP’s liability. The total debt and liabilities is made up of borrowings in rupees from the SBP, banks, national savings schemes, prize bonds, Sukuk etc., and borrowings in foreign currency from multilateral institutions such as the World Bank, ADB, IDB, bilateral governments or global financial markets in the form of Eurobonds or Sukuk.

Rupee-denominated borrowing is termed ‘domestic debt’ and foreign currency-denominated borrowing ‘external debt’. Domestic debt risks are different from those of the external debt. Lumping them together is analytically incorrect. While both create debt-servicing liability for budgetary purposes and thus affect fiscal balances, the risk profile of each is quite different. Domestic debt has to be paid in rupees, which can be printed, or the central bank can acquire those obligations on its balance sheet by creating reserve money. It involves creating possible inflationary pressures but there is no risk of default — a real threat in case of foreign currency-denominated debt. Countries that have suffered debt crises have faced solvency and liquidity risks in servicing their foreign currency loans. Risks from domestic debt include rollover risk, interest rate risk, and crowding out of private-sector credit. Here, we’ll focus largely on external debt and liabilities and its servicing.

The reform journey to increase exports, investment and productivity must be accelerated.

Pakistan’s external debt and liabilities amount to $139 billion, of which public sector debt accounts for almost two-thirds and the private sector one-third. In the public sector, direct government debt is 80pc of the total. What are the diagnostics of vulnerability indicators of the stock of EDL and debt-servicing capacity? First is the break-up between medium- and long-term and short-term loans. In our case, the ratio is: 88 MLT and 12 ST. Official liquid reserves are enough to cover the ST loans and loans maturing during the year. However, the rollover of friendly country deposits next year will go up to $12bn again. Second is concessionality — the average interest rate, years to maturity, and proportion of fixed rate loans. The higher the element of concessionality, the stronger the safety valve. Fifty per cent of loans are concessional, showing a downward slide from the past ratios. Other stock indicators don’t look healthy. Third, EDL-to-GDP ratio has moved from 24pc to 31pc in the last decade. Fourth, EDL-to-export of goods and services too has worsened — from 210 to 340. Fifth, EDL-to-foreign exchange earnings shows an upward movement from 100 to 168 — not a satisfactory trend. Sixth, EDL-to-foreign exchange reserves has shot up alarmingly from 350 to 750, despite a build-up of reserves in the last two years.

Debt-servicing indicators show that external debt servicing-to-GDP has risen from 1.7pc to 4pc, while EDS-to-exports of goods and services has more than doubled from 18pc to 44pc. So has EDS-to-foreign exchange earnings from 10pc to 22pc and EDS-to-foreign exchange reserves from 37pc to 98pc.

This picture shows that to exit the IMF programme after October 2027, palliative measures are needed over the next two years to relieve the debt situation and build up capacity to absorb shocks. There are four levers to reduce the ratios: a) faster growth of exports and foreign exchange earnings; b) faster GDP growth in US dollars; c) lower current account deficits; and (d) lower interest and refinancing costs via concessional financing and maturity extension.

Assuming 4pc GDP growth in FY27-29, inflation contained at 6.5pc, fiscal deficit of 2.9pc and primary surplus of 2pc, the target should be to bring the debt-to-GDP ratio to 60pc and external debt-to-GDP ratio to 25pc by FY29 by implementing these policy measures: a) export of goods to reach $40bn rather than $36bn — a $4bn increase; b) import of goods to reach $76bn instead of $79bn — savings of $3bn; c) export of services to move up to $12bn instead of $11bn — a $1bn increase; d) workers’ remittances to go up to $46bn instead of $43bn — an increase of $3bn; and e) an FDI of $3.7bn rather than $2.7bn — a jump of $1bn.

The reform journey to increase exports, investment and productivity must be accelerated. The list of delayed and deferred decisions is long. To mention a few — reducing the tax burden and overregulation of manufacturing and export, upgrading oil refineries, third-party access to oil exploration companies, introduction of weighted average cost of gas, opening up retail electricity and gas business to the private sector, elimination of cross-subsidy from industrial to domestic consumers rather than targeting through BISP, the ML-I railway track (announced in 2015), the Sukkur-Hyderabad motorway, increased share of railway freight traffic, tax collection under agriculture income tax, property tax, GST on professional services, operationalising Exim Bank for export financing and insurance, streamlining FBR’s export facilitation scheme, expeditious ref­u­­nds to exporters, increasing productivity of small­­holder agriculture, financial access for SMEs, agriculture, low-cost housing, and SEZs for CPEC 2.0. The announcement and implementation of the industrial policy can help achieve the outlined increases and savings in the external account.

The amount of $12bn can be used for liquidating the bilateral deposits if they are not swapped for equity in long gestation investment projects or their maturities are not extended to the long term. By FY29, the removal of this Damocles sword over our heads should be able to moderate the vulnerability indicators discussed earlier. We don’t have to seek another loan from the IMF and can regain our economic sovereignty.

The writer is a former State Bank governor.

Published in Dawn, September 3rd, 2026

title: Diplomatic success
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S star in the field of foreign policy is on the ascendant. Not too long ago, because of our own mistakes and the malevolence of some in the neighbourhood, Pakistan’s reputation had suffered internationally. That situation has changed. Today, in the region and the world, Pakistan is recognised for its diplomatic finesse, for bringing together adversaries, and for contributing to regional peace. Yet for all the accolades, the country can only capitalise on this improved reputation by addressing the internal hurdles holding it back from the path of progress.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif was recently in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, to attend the SCO Council of Heads of State summit. Pakistan has assumed the SCO chair and the next summit will be held in Islamabad. At the event, Mr Sharif met with leaders from within the Eurasian bloc, including those of Russia and China. Just before the summit, the first formal meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance was held in Istanbul.

At this forum too, Pakistan’s relevance on the global stage was highlighted — this country has been chosen to head the pact’s secretariat. The pact itself is the extension of last year’s defence agreement signed with the Saudis; that development, too, had attracted global attention. But perhaps the biggest diplomatic coup Pakistan has pulled off in the recent past was to bring Iran and the US to the negotiating table in Islamabad in April. While violence has again flared between these two states, the global consensus remains that the Islamabad MoU offers the best path to peace.

All of these laurels are well-earned, as Pakistan’s leadership has gone the extra mile to promote peace in the region. However, the true value of these diplomatic successes can only be realised when there is peace and prosperity within. Internally, the challenges remain formidable. Pakistan faces two major terrorist insurgencies in KP and Balochistan. Meanwhile, though the economic situation is now comparatively stable to what it had been not too long ago, the country is still far from the path of sustainable growth.

Political instability is another major concern. Unless space is granted to all political forces in Pakistan, stability will elude us. The PM also spoke of the importance of regional connectivity in Bishkek. Regional integration is key, but when Pakistan faces two hostile neighbours — India to the east and Taliban-ruled Afghanistan to the west — as well as a war in Iran and the Gulf, achieving this integration becomes challenging.

While Pakistan can again extend the hand of friendship to New Delhi and Kabul, much depends on how these states respond, while the situation in the Gulf is beyond Pakistan’s control. What can be done is to address internal matters such as security, economic policy and political reconciliation.

Published in Dawn, September 3rd, 2026

title: Regulatory failure
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
WHEN a regulator fails to do its job, the consequences are felt by everyone, even if in ways too subtle to notice directly. The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) is the apex regulator for all financial markets and incorporated companies in the country. Next to it is the front-line regulator, the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX), whose job is to regulate listed companies and trading activity on the stock market floor. And the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) is the main regulator for all banks.

It is the job of these three entities to ensure that companies under their watch are not breaking the law, or taking risks that threaten systemic stability, or concealing material information from their shareholders (in the case of listed companies), or engaging in insider trading. The job is not easy and requires constant vigilance. It also requires moral courage.

What reportedly happened at Unity Foods, a listed company operating in edible oil and rice, now in the crosshairs of the FIA, was a stark example of regulatory failure. The company is accused of having discrepancies totalling more than Rs44 billion between its published accounts and internal record. The SECP reportedly smelled trouble in the company as far back as 2019, but ran into legal hurdles in its efforts to try and investigate. By the time the investigation finally concluded and enough material was gathered to merit accusations of alleged criminal liability, almost six years had passed.

The big problem here is the sanctity of accounts of listed companies that are publicly owned and traded. In the case of Unity Foods, the biggest shareholder happened to be a Singapore-based company called Wilmar International, which announced earlier this year that they have taken a loss of $150 million on their books due to their investment in Pakistan. Their statement said the audited statements they were shown by company management all along appeared to show profitability and healthy material assets. Then, in 2025, the company began having difficulty servicing its bank debts, leading to questions from the Board, and the eventual departure of its CEO and founder in December 2025, followed by its CFO in January. Since then, Wilmar said it discovered a string of inconsistencies on the company’s books in financial and working capital items, leading ultimately to an FIR a few days ago.

If regulators can’t detect malpractices until a company’s solvency is in doubt, then why would investors feel safe putting their money in the country?

The bigger story here is the hit that Pakistan’s corporate governance framework takes with this episode. If this could happen in a listed company, overseen by two highly staffed regulators (the PSX and SECP), and auditors could sign off on the company’s health one year, only for criminal charges to be filed against massive discrepancies between its published and internal data to be discovered a year later, then what does it say for the quality of our regulators and auditors?

This episode shows why investment, whether foreign or domestic, is so difficult to arrange in Pakistan. If two regulators and an auditing firm can fail to detect these kinds of malpractices for so long, until the company has reached a point where its solvency is in doubt, then how is an investor supposed to feel confident about putting money down in Pakistan with long repayment horizons? And this is only the most extreme example of regulatory failure.

Consider another problem that is brewing in our banking industry but has not yet detonated into a crisis. Everyone knows that one bank is so overextended in the amounts it has borrowed short term from the State Bank that it is today the single most concentrated source of systemic risk that the financial system has seen. The bank’s borrowing from the short-term window known as Open Market Operations (OMO) is now larger than its total deposit base, meaning it owes more to the SBP than it does to its own depositors. I cannot recall a similar situation in our financial history, at least not over the last quarter of a century.

In the last three years, its borrowing from the OMO window went from six per cent of the total to more than 50pc today. From around the summer of 2023, the SBP’s OMO book grew by Rs5.5 trillion, and the bank took on more than 100pc of this. Read that again. Not only did the SBP grow its entire OMO book by a staggering amount, injecting all that money into the monetary system, but it also allowed one bank to soak up all of it, as well as whatever was rolling off the books of other banks.

More than 97pc of this borrowing from the OMO window was set to mature between one to seven days in the bank’s last annual report. Nobody knows whether this maturity structure has changed much in the last eight or nine months. This is disturbing. The bank is refinancing its entire SBP position almost every week. The amount that is at stake is more than 10 times its total equity.

Clearly, this situation is untenable. Yes, the build-up is secured against government paper and does not present default risk in the narrow sense. But if the SBP has to stop rolling this mess over, or if there is an external shock that forces a rate hike for example, it could force a fire sale of this same government paper into a market that cannot absorb them, at a bank whose equity is a tiny fraction of the total position. The central bank has lent itself into a corner, and nobody there seems to be asking any questions about this. Its OMO book is how the SBP manages market liquidity, and today almost half of it is held by one bank, that cannot repay without liquidating itself. This is also regulatory failure.

The writer is a business and economy journalist.

Published in Dawn, September 3rd, 2026

title: Rights in jail
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE Islamabad High Court earlier this week ruled on two petitions challenging the conditions in which former prime minister Imran Khan and former first lady Bushra Bibi have been kept in Adiala Jail, ordering the jail superintendent to ensure they receive the privileges they are entitled to as prisoners and that neither is kept in isolation.

It is disturbing to note that though jail officials and government representatives have consistently denied allegations that the two prisoners are being held in solitary confinement for extended periods, medical records submitted by the authorities indicate that the former prime minister has started suffering physically from the effects of isolation. Indeed, the court noted that “the admitted fact remains that access of the general prison population to his place of confinement is substantially restricted and his meaningful social interaction is consequently limited”, and that the record “prima facie recognises the adverse impact of restricted social and familial interaction upon the prisoner’s psychological and physical well-being”.

As the court rightly noted, a prisoner’s right to life, dignity and humane treatment “are not extinguished at the prison gate”. This, in particular, seems to be something that those running the Pakistani penal system have never quite wrapped their heads around. Human beings cannot be mistreated, even when they have erred. The law may prescribe the most severe punishment for their crimes, but that does not mean prisoners can be treated by their jailers as they see fit.

Unfortunately, most Pakistani prisoners are frequently made to suffer far more than what is just or right. The injustices done to them are also very rarely remedied. Therefore, for a once powerful leader to be made to suffer in this manner is merely a symptom of a much larger disease. Our penal system needs much more than one-time interventions to address its maladies; it needs to be rebuilt as an instrument of justice rather than remain a means of inflicting pain.

title: Moving upstream
author: none@none.com (Salma Khan)
content:
IMAGINE someone in Pakistan is standing at a counter this morning. She is being told that the system will not accept her name as it appears on her degree. Her name on the degree is spelled differently, and the database will only accept the name in the format already stored against her identity record. The clerk is not difficult; the field on the digital form will not take it. There is no form for objection and no hearing at which she can explain that both names belong to the same person.

In this hypothetical scenario, a decision about her legal identity has just been made by a database. When a state moves from paper to software, a lot more changes than just the speed at which things are done.

For most of our history, law lived in a medium we understood: the register, the file, the stamped deed, the court record. A lawyer’s authority came from mastering that medium: what the text said, what a court had made it mean, and how to work out the space between the two. On paper, a rule takes effect through interpretation. An official reads it; someone contests it; a judge decides.

In a system, the rule is executed. The database either lets that department see your record, or it does not. Nobody necessarily weighs your circumstances at the moment of decision unless somebody deliberately built that pause into the design.

Pakistan’s digital state needs a new kind of lawyer — one who stops treating the system as somebody else’s department.

Pakistan is now building at pace. The Digital Nation Pakistan Act, 2025, created the Pakistan Digital Authority, with a mandate covering digital governance, data, artificial intelligence and digital public infrastructure. The draft National Data Governance Policy, 2026, declares government data a strategic national asset and proposes rules on data sovereignty, and cross-border transfers. In April, the National Judicial (Policy­making) Committee issued guidelines positioning AI as an assistive tool for judicial institutions.

Meanwhile, the Personal Data Protection Bill remains a draft, years after the 2018 version was published.

So, the architecture is arriving ahead of the supposed governing law. Therefore, it is safe to assume that for now governance will largely come from policy documents, procurement contracts and default settings. This means lawyers will increasingly need to be involved not just when something goes wrong, but when these systems are being designed and built in the first place.

Consider interoperability, which is the quiet centre of all of this. A service links records, so a citizen no longer submits information the state already holds. That makes life easier, but it also creates important legal questions. Who may open that record, and for what purpose? How long does an incorrect entry follow someone, and who is answerable for it? What is left of consent when refusing to share means losing a service you need? Those are legal questions with technical answers, and technical questions with legal consequences.

Legal practice is forming around them. Data governance is the most visible piece: someone has to negotiate the terms on which institutions share, secure and delete individuals’ data, and that work happens before a system is built, not afterwards.

Artificial intelligence adds another layer. The National AI Policy, 2025, and the Islamabad AI Declaration both put accountability alongside adoption. This sounds unobjectionable until you have to demonstrate it. A lawyer in this space needs to know how a model was tested, where it fails, and what record would satisfy a regulator two years later. Much of the work is about evidence rather than doctrine.

Then there is the lawyer who sits with the people building the thing. The old sequence was linear: a team builds, legal clears. What is emerging moves counsel upstream, into the design conversation. Suppose a rule says an AI system must be auditable. Somebody has to decide what gets logged, who may inspect it, and what triggers review. An engineer cannot decide that alone, because the obligation is legal. A lawyer cannot decide it alone either, because the answer is a specification.

That shift also changes where legal judgement enters the process. It is no longer enough to ask whether a policy is lawful on paper. The important question is whether the institution has translated that policy into workflows that behave lawfully when nobody is watching. That means understanding exceptions, escalation paths, audit trails, access controls, and people who are affected when the system gets something wrong. It is a different kind of legal practice, but it is legal practice.

If I had to name one skill for the next generation, it would be that act of translation. A regulator can declare that an automated decision must be accountable. A policymaker can create a right to human review. A right nobody has built into a system is, in practice, a right that does not exist. Carrying a principle down into a requirement, a control, and a record somebody can check is now part of what it means to make the law work.

None of this threatens traditional practice. We will always need formidable litigators and lawyers who can draft contracts. But the surrounding literacy is shifting. How data moves through an institution, what an interface actually does, how digital identity works, where security risk collects. Lawyers do not need to write code. Lawyers do need to stop treating the system as somebody else’s department.

The question worth asking is not whether technology will replace lawyers. It is whether lawyers will be in the room when these systems are designed.

Pakistan is laying the foundations of a digital state. Its rules are being written now, some in statutes, and a great many in software.

The writer is a technology lawyer specialising in data protection.

title: Azad Kashmir saga
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
REJECTED by voters in his own constituency, lawyer Iftikhar Gillani has been chosen as the new prime minister of Azad Jammu & Kashmir. A local PML-N leader, he was elected on a reserved seat for technocrats after losing in the recently held regional elections. His nomination caught even his own party by surprise. Gillani, who had also lost the last election, is not the electorate’s choice — so, whose nominee is he?

It is an unprecedented choice even in a place where governments are made and removed from outside. But why should it surprise anyone, given the state of democracy in this area? While voicing other demands, the legitimacy of elections, which were held in the midst of a popular uprising in parts of AJK, has been questioned — even by mainstream parties like the PPP. Gillani was not nominated for the post by the party’s local chapter; he was picked by the PML-N central leadership in Lahore. Yet, he could not have been elected to the top-most position in this highly sensitive and troubled region without the blessing of the powers that be.

Gillani’s election in defiance of democratic norms reinforces the contention that the reserved seats are tools for manipulating the system and installing a government of the choice of Pakistan-based political parties and the establishment. The PML-N has emerged as the single-largest political party in the controversial elections, helped by the eight seats for Kashmiri refugees in Punjab. Polling could not be held on seven seats in Rawalakot and some other districts because of the continuing protests by the outlawed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), leaving the House incomplete.

It has now been more than three months since the group — comprising mainly youth, traders, and other sections of society — took to the streets with various demands, including the abolition of the refugee seats. The demand was not new; it had been raised regularly by other political parties in the past but was never heeded. Many of those elected on these seats had questionable bona fides yet held ministerial posts. The sham has cast doubt on the entire democratic process in AJK.

Controversial polls and the installation of an indirectly elected PM were bound to fuel anger.

There has been a media blackout on news from the troubled districts, where several people have reportedly been killed in violent clashes with law-enforcement agencies. The government has barred international media from the area after an Al Jazeera report showed violence and low turnout at the elections. Human rights groups have also been prevented from visiting the troubled districts. Protesters have continued to hold their ground. Internet and mobile services have been disconnected for months. These punitive measures and the state’s use of coercive methods have alienated the population.

Against this background, the controversial elections and the installation of an indirectly elected prime minister were bound to fuel public anger. The very perception of an unrepresentative government being propped up risks complicating the country’s stated support for Kashmir’s right to self-determination. Kashmiri leaders everywhere have expressed concern over the rights situation.

The protests have also reverberated in Britain, which is home to a large Kashmiri diaspora drawn mainly from the troubled districts. Many Muslim MPs are descendants of migrants from Mirpur, which has also witnessed protests along with other districts. Protest rallies have been reported in recent weeks in front of the Pakistan High Commission in London. The Kashmiri community in Britain is the main voice against the Indian occupation of Jammu and Kashmir. It is also the main source of remittances from Britain to Pakistan. The use of force to silence those demanding basic rights carries the risk of eroding the community’s support.

The controversy surrounding the latest elections, and the installation of a prime minister rejected by his own constituency will only reinforce concerns that local autonomy is being undermined. The irony is that those raising their voice against undemocratic practices are being branded as anti-state, as seen in the recent measure to ban a civic platform like the JAAC.

Under these conditions, it will be difficult for the AJK government, headed by a leader who has yet to prove his credentials, to handle a grave political crisis. Many view the arrangement as an overreach by the centre, which could create complications for the state’s principled position on the Kashmir dispute.

The picture reflects the autocratic mindset of a hybrid dispensation which routinely resorts to kinetic means to crush protests in the country. The state must learn its lesson from the eruption of public discontent and not repeat its mistakes in Azad Kashmir. Local autonomy must be respected so that the Kashmiris can decide their own future, without being subjected to arrangements that have been shaped from the outside.

The use of force is never the solution in any situation; political reconciliation and the restoration of democratic rights, not only in Azad Kashmir but also in Pakistan are the need of the hour. Unlike genuinely representative governments, imposed set-ups do not have the capacity to deal with serious challenges. Kashmiris living under Indian occupation across the Line of Control, have always looked towards Pakistan in their struggle for the right to self-determination. That trust must be preserved.

Meanwhile, instead of banning the JAAC, the state would have been better off trying to resolve the crisis through negotiations. There is no time to lose. Further delay in redressing matters could push the situation to a point of no-return.

The writer is an author and journalist.zhussain100@yahoo.comX: @hidhussain
