title: Wrong solution to the right problem
author: none@none.com (Ahmad Hassan)
content:
PAKISTAN’S governance crisis is fundamentally institutional rather than geographical.
While the creation of new provinces may address certain concerns relating to regional identity, representation, and administrative reach, it cannot by itself remedy systemic deficiencies in governance. Without meaningful institutional reform, decentralisation, and fiscal planning, new provinces risk reproducing existing problems at a greater administrative and financial cost.
Modern federal democracies increasingly function through a three-tier system of governance, in which constitutional authority is distributed among the federal government, provincial governments and elected local governments. The rationale is both democratic and practical; decisions should be taken at the lowest level capable of addressing them effectively.
National defence and foreign affairs belong to the federation, provincial policy belongs to the provinces while matters such as municipal services, sanitation, local infrastructure and community development are most effectively managed by local governments. This principle of democratic decentralisation ensures that government remains closer, more responsive and more accountable to the people.
Pakistan’s Constitution already embraces this model. Article 140A requires provinces to establish local governments and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility to elected local representatives.
In other words, the Constitution already provides a mechanism for bringing government closer to the people. The challenge, therefore, is not the absence of a constitutional framework but the failure to implement it meaningfully.
    
Unfortunately, Pakistan’s experience has often been the opposite. Local governments have frequently been weakened, dissolved or deprived of meaningful financial autonomy, while development funds and administrative authority remain concentrated at the provincial level.
This is, in part, a consequence of the political incentive structure within provincial governance. Meaningful devolution inevitably reduces the concentration of power, resources and political visibility enjoyed by the provincial leadership, creating little incentive to transfer genuine authority to local institutions.
The consequence is a constitutional distortion. Members of the provincial assemblies, instead of focusing on legislation, policy formulation, executive oversight and public finance, increasingly involve themselves in roads, schools, local development schemes and other matters of municipal administration.
Legislators are elected to make laws and hold the executive accountable, not to perform functions that properly belong to elected local governments. When legislative institutions assume executive responsibilities, both governance and lawmaking suffer.
The question is whether good governance will be achieved by creating more provinces or by strengthening the institutions that already exist.
Before creating additional provinces, Pakistan must therefore ask why the existing constitutional model of local government has not been fully implemented. If governance is the primary objective, strengthening local governments may prove to be a more effective and less costly reform than creating entirely new provincial structures.
Another aspect that merits consideration is the financial implications of creating new provinces. A province is not merely a new chief minister and provincial assembly. It requires a complete governmental framework, including a high court, provincial secretariat, public service institutions, tax authorities, police administration, regulatory bodies, specialised departments and thousands of public servants. These institutions create permanent financial obligations in terms of salaries, pensions, infrastructure and operational costs.
    
The question is not whether Pakistan can create new provinces. It can. The question is whether the anticipated governance benefits justify the substantial administrative and financial costs.
Another important consideration is economic sustainability. Many proposed provinces, particularly less industrialised regions, possess significant agricultural potential but limited industrial and service-sector capacity. Without a diversified economic base, newly created provinces may remain heavily dependent on federal transfers for their survival. Therefore, any restructuring of provincial boundaries must be preceded by serious fiscal analysis.
This is not an argument against creating new provinces. It is an argument that constitutional restructuring must be accompanied by institutional and financial planning.
The identity dimension of this debate must also not be forgotten. For many communities, demands for new provinces are not only about administration but also about recognition, representation and political inclusion. Historical regions such as Bahawalpur and Hazara have long sought acknowledgment of their distinct identities. Such aspirations cannot simply be dismissed.
However, political representation must translate into actual improvement in the lives of citizens. Creating new provinces may provide opportunities for regional leadership and address feelings of exclusion, but changing boundaries alone cannot resolve deeper issues of governance, economic opportunity, institutional capacity and public service delivery.
Pakistan’s governance challenges require a comprehensive approach. Strong local governments, professional civil services, transparent administration, fiscal responsibility and constitutional continuity are the foundations of effective governance.
    
If, after meaningful reforms and careful fiscal assessment, parliament concludes that additional provinces are necessary, such decisions should be taken on constitutional and administrative grounds rather than political expediency.
Pakistan undoubtedly needs better governance. The question is whether that objective will be achieved by creating more provinces or by strengthening the institutions that already exist.
The problems undermining governance are not merely products of geography. Before redrawing the map, we should first reform the machinery that governs it.
The writer is a practising lawyer based in Lahore.

title: The supreme sacrifice
author: none@none.com (Afzal Ali ShigriTariq ParvezTariq Khosa)
content:
THE police are a vital pillar of our social fabric, serving not only as guardians of the law but also as protectors of the community, said President Asif Ali Zardari on Police Martyrs Day on Aug 4. “Their exemplary courage, firm dedication and ultimate sacrifice in the service of the nation will always inspire pride and command the deepest respect of every citizen of Pakistan,” he added. The prime minister, too, honoured the bravery of police officers who had laid down their lives in the line of duty, noting that the force displays “exceptional professionalism and unflinching resolve” in the nation’s fight against terrorism, violent extremism and crime.
The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies reported that the first seven months of 2026 witnessed 2,786 deaths linked to terrorist violence and counterterrorism operations — 434 security forces’ personnel lost their lives, including 152 police officials in KP and 89 in Balochistan. So far, July has been the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security officials offering the supreme sacrifice in the line of duty, compared to 38 fatalities a month earlier in June. This is an unprecedented 195 per cent increase in the deaths of law enforcers. 
At least eight suicide attacks were recorded last month, the highest number in a single month during the past decade. The recent deadly attack near a police station in Swat caused 17 fatalities. As this paper rightly asserted after the Swat bombing, it “is far too high a toll, and the state needs to urgently refine its CT strategy to prevent further loss of precious lives”.
Following Police Martyrs Day, one of us convened a forum of serving and retired police officers to discuss the current vulnerabilities and challenges faced by police in general, and those in KP and Balochistan in particular. The trajectory and tenor of violence in these provinces have distinct traits. KP has been on the receiving end since 9/11, paying a huge price in the so-called war against terror. Since Kabul’s takeover by the Taliban in August 2021, violence and bloodshed have assumed greater intensity. Acts of terror have risen exponentially, with fatalities among security forces and civilians progressively rising each year. The last two years have been the worst so far, with police losing 314 personnel.
The last two years have been the worst so far, with police losing 314 personnel.
Balochistan is facing its fifth (and longest) phase (20 years) of insurgency by separatists. Nawab Akbar Bugti’s killing in a cave near Kohlu in August 2006 was an unfortunate incident that led to a sharp escalation in Baloch militancy. The terrorist nexus of the BLA, BRA and BLF has added lethality to insurgent attacks. BLA’s Majeed Brigade is well-equipped and emulates TTP’s violent tactics. It has superior weaponry, indicating the role of hostile foreign agencies in fomenting unrest in the province. The police’s challenge has increased manifold now that the entire province has been converted into police jurisdiction. The gap in human resources, infrastructure and training for the job is pronounced. A recent significant development is the incursion of the TTP in the Pakhtun areas as witnessed in the tragic July 6 attack on the Mangi Dam pumping station police post by the terrorist group, leading to the kidnapping and killing of 27 policemen. Our deliberations have led to identification of certain vulnerabilities and constraints that beset the police operating in the terror and insurgency-prone areas of KP and Balochistan where violence is driven by a combination of enhanced militant capability, difficult terrain, cross-border dynamics and institutional challenges. The following issues are pertinent.
Intelligence coordination and information sharing: Coordination between police, intel agencies and other law-enforcement institutions is not always seamless; delays in sharing actionable intelligence reduce the ability to prevent attacks or intercept terrorists before they strike.
Inadequate protection of police personnel and infrastructure: Police stations, check posts and patrols are often targeted because they have limited physical protection, surveillance or early-warning capabilities; some units in dangerous zones lack sufficient protective equipment, secure transport and modern communication systems, increasing their vulnerability.
Limited capacity and community-based policing: In remote and conflict-affected areas, a trust deficit exists between communities and police. Without strong local engagement, authorities receive fewer timely reports about suspicious activities, allowing terrorist networks to operate with greater freedom.
The merger of Fata into KP and the conversion of ‘B’ areas into ‘A’ areas in Balochistan was undertaken without adequate planning, capacity building or the provision of necessary financial and operational resources. The denial of these essential resources has exposed both police and the civil armed forces to avoidable risks, contributing to a significant increase in casualties among personnel. Expressions of support and appreciation for their sacrifices must therefore be matched by meaningful investment in manpower, training, equipment, intelligence, mobility and welfare to enable police to perform their duties effectively and safely.
As former police chiefs we acknowledge that the challenges faced by current police commanders are far more daunting and require a strategic and operational rethink to restore order and promote peace in the restive borderlands in Pakistan’s north and south. Serving and retired police officers agree that the revised CT NAP must be implemented through professional tactics and strategic oversight. Here are a few recommendations at the operational level.
Strengthen intelligence-led policing: Establish integrated intelligence coordination mechanisms that facilitate timely information-sharing among police, intelligence services and local administration; expand analytical capabilities and use technology to identify emerging threats, while ensuring operations remain consistent with the law and human rights standards.
Modernise police protection and training: Upgrade security at vulnerable police facilities through better surveillance, convoy drills, ambush response, communications and sound infrastructure; provide regular training in CT tactics, drone threat response, incident command and officer safety, along with appropriate protective equipment.
Expand community policing and public partnerships: Build stronger relationships with local communities, tribal elders, religious leaders and CSOs to improve trust and encourage lawful reporting of suspicious activities; develop accessible mechanisms for citizens to share information confidentially; promote public awareness programmes that strengthen resilience.
The trend of rising terrorist attacks against, and thus higher casualties among, the police must be immediately stopped before it derails the entire CT effort in KP and Balochistan. This requires a balanced approach that combines effective policing, better intelligence coordination, professional training and meaningful community engagement. Strengthening these areas can enhance the safety of police personnel while also increasing public confidence and contributing to a more secure environment for local communities. Finally, for the policymakers and political leadership, our message is simple: invest in police and trust them to deliver. 
The writers are former inspectors-general of police.

title: Before AI hits the grid
author: none@none.com (Mahwish Khan)
content:
PAKISTAN’S announcement that it would allocate 2,000 megawatts of electricity for Bitcoin mining and AI data centres has triggered a predictable debate: can the country afford to supply that much power? It is an important question, but not the most useful one. Bitcoin mining, AI training and real-time digital services do not exactly place identical demands on the electricity system.
Pakistan’s electricity challenge is about more than the amount of generation capacity available. It is about when and where electricity is needed, whether the network can deliver it reliably, and how that demand is managed during periods of stress. During the hottest months, cooling demand pushes the grid towards its limits. At other times, generation capacity remains underused. But nationally available capacity does not automatically translate into reliable electricity at the location and hour a data centre requires it. Transmission constraints, substation capacity and power quality matter just as much as the headline allocation.
The better question is this: how should this new demand be designed and integrated into the electricity system from the outset?
Data centres are not ordinary consumers. Their location, cooling systems, computing equipment and grid connections are decided before construction begins. That gives Pakistan a rare opportunity to shape a major new category of demand before it becomes embedded in the system. But doing so requires recognising that not all computing demand is the same. Some services are highly sensitive to delay. User-facing AI applications, financial platforms and communications systems may require continuous availability. Their loads cannot simply be switched off whenever the grid comes under pressure. Other workloads may offer more flexibility. Certain forms of data processing and model training can be scheduled within broader time windows, distributed across locations or paused at planned checkpoints, depending on how the systems are designed.
Pakistan’s electricity challenge is about more than the amount of generation capacity available.
Where genuine flexibility exists, it can be reflected in tariffs and connection agreements. Eligible workloads could be scheduled outside critical peak hours. Operators could provide more accurate demand forecasts, limit abrupt changes in consumption, or use storage to reduce pressure on the network during short periods of stress. This is not a hypothetical mechanism. The UN referred to Ireland as a “cautionary tale” when the country faced a severe energy crisis because data centres consume roughly 23 per cent of the nation’s total electricity — nearly rivalling the power used by all residential homes combined. Ireland’s grid operator now assesses new data centre connections in constrained areas partly on whether the applicant can prove its demand is flexible, and writes that commitment directly into the connection agreement rather than leaving it voluntary. Pakistan can build the same discipline in from the start, instead of retrofitting it once the grid is already under strain, the way Ireland had to.
Pakistan does not need to begin from scratch. The country already has a cloud-governance and accreditation framework. The Cloud Office is mandated to set standards and compliance requirements for cloud service providers, while the existing accreditation criteria cover security, service availability, resilient power infrastructure and recognised data centre certification.
What the framework does not yet fully address is how efficiently these facilities use electricity and water, or how they interact with the wider power system.
The Ministry of IT & Telecom’s own concept note identifies this gap. It notes that the current framework does not explicitly prescribe standards for energy management, environmental performance, power usage effectiveness, water usage effectiveness or renewable energy integration. It proposes a national sustainability framework for data centres to fill that gap. That is the right direction. But the framework should go one step further by connecting digital-infrastructure planning with power sector planning.
Large facilities should provide credible forecasts of their electricity and water demand. Projects should be assessed against local network capacity, not simply national generation figures. Energy and water performance should be measured consistently. And tariffs should reward verified efficiency and flexibility rather than merely offering cheap electricity to large consumers.
This is not anti-investment. Serious data centre investors already consider reliable power, cooling, environmental compliance and long-term energy security when choosing markets. Good standards are not a barrier to investment, but rather, a part of a credible investment proposition. The first generation of AI infrastructure will shape the one that follows. Early decisions on location, efficiency and grid connection will become precedents that are harder to change once major investments have been made.
Pakistan does not need to wait for its grid to buckle before it asks this question, the way Ireland did. It has the chance to design demand before it hits the grid, not renegotiate it after the fact. 
The writer is director, Awareness and Outreach, National Energy Efficiency & Conservation Authority.
Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

title: Danger ahead
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN has already paid a heavy human price this monsoon, even as another dangerous spell approaches. NDMA figures covering June 26 to Aug 7 record 151 deaths — 73 of them children — and 448 injuries, besides damage to more than 1,200 houses and dozens of bridges and kilometres of roads. Chitral shows how quickly such destruction multiplies into other emergencies. Glofs, cloudbursts and flash floods have washed away bridges and severed roads, leaving communities unable to reach healthcare. Attendance at Lower Chitral’s district headquarters hospital has fallen by around 55pc, while patients from some isolated villages have stopped arriving altogether. Doctors are already reporting gastroenteritis and dysentery and fear outbreaks of typhoid and malaria. Pregnant women unable to reach hospitals face particular danger, while post-traumatic stress is emerging among disaster-hit communities. The situation shows us how extreme weather kills not only through torrents and collapsing homes, but also by cutting people off from medicines, clean water and timely treatment.
NDMA, Rescue 1122, district administrations and the National Highway Authority have been involved in evacuations, relief distribution and restoration work. But each disaster exposes the distance between issuing warnings and protecting people. Chitral residents have complained of slow road clearance, delaying access to villages where medical needs are mounting. Warning equipment in parts of KP has previously been damaged or stolen, pointing to weaknesses in maintenance and local ownership. District authorities must know which settlements require evacuation, where residents will be taken, how alerts will get to people without mobile connectivity and how food, medicines and medical teams will reach communities. Such plans must be prepared before an emergency, not improvised after valleys are cut off. Medical camps, safe-water points and emergency stocks should be positioned in vulnerable valleys.
There is particular urgency now. PMD’s Aug 7 outlook warns of moderate to heavy rainfall over the upper catchments of all major rivers from Aug 10 to 13, including KP, GB, Azad Kashmir, Islamabad and upper Punjab, with river and tributary flows expected to rise. Authorities should use this window to pre-position heavy machinery, boats, temporary bridges, fuel, food, drinking water, medicines and mobile clinics. Pregnant women, elderly people and patients requiring regular treatment should be identified for early evacuation, while alternative communication systems must be ready where conventional networks may fail. Shelters should be accessible and evacuation routes communicated before conditions deteriorate. Pakistan cannot control the monsoon or the instability of its glaciers. But it can control how seriously it acts on warnings. With the warning already given, the task now is to ensure that the next spell does not deepen an already heavy human toll.
Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

title: Israeli impunity
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
ANY hope that Hamas’s decision to disarm would lead to a breakthrough has been dashed for one simple reason: Israeli impunity. Tel Aviv has reacted to the Palestinian group’s announcement by saying it would not withdraw from Gaza until there was ‘genuine’ disarmament. What this actually means is that Israel has no intention of ending the occupation. Frustration at the Zionist state’s intransigence has been expressed by eight Muslim states, including Pakistan, that recently issued a statement condemning Tel Aviv’s violence in Gaza. Israeli attacks on health facilities and civilian targets were particularly highlighted in the statement, whose signatories include Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkiye. According to Unicef, Israel has killed 300 children over the last 300 days. Such a ‘ceasefire’, the UN agency said, “is failing children”. Meanwhile, the situation in the occupied West Bank is not any better, with violent settler attacks continuing. The settler community in Israel is known for its extremism and use of violence against Arab civilians. They aim to uproot the Palestinians from their ancestral lands and cement the occupation. While the Israeli state claims to investigate such attacks, this means little when rabid supporters of the settler movement sit in the cabinet. The statement by Muslim states also highlighted the situation in the West Bank.
The Muslim states have urged the UN Security Council to compel Israel to fulfil its obligations. This is wishful thinking, because if the UN and the international community had played their role, there would have been no campaign of extermination in Gaza, and the tens of thousands of Palestinians murdered by Israel since 2023 would have been alive today. If the Muslim world wants to end the carnage in Gaza and the West Bank, it must take practical steps against Israel, such as a diplomatic and trade boycott. Resolutions and condemnations will not save the Palestinians from Israeli terror. Moreover, President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace must be asked what it aims to do to make Israel honour the Gaza peace deal. It is clear that Tel Aviv does not intend to stop its murderous campaign in the Strip. The Palestinians have been making concessions for peace. It is now time Israel’s Western benefactors asked it to put its money where its mouth is.

title: Pakistan’s privacy debate
author: none@none.com (Salma Khan)
content:
EVERY discussion about data protection in Pakistan reaches the same conclusion: we still don’t have a comprehensive data privacy law.
Technically, that’s true. The Personal Data Protection Bill has sat in draft form since 2018, and after years of delay it’s easy to assume Pakistan’s approach to data governance is on hold.
That assumption can now be challenged.
    
While attention stayed fixed on the stalled privacy bill, another development moved far faster. In late June, the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) released the draft National Data Governance Policy 2026 for public consultation. That consultation closed on July 10. This week, MoITT and the Pakistan Digital Authority (PDA) held a high-level meeting, chaired by Federal Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja, to finalise the policy ahead of cabinet approval and gazette notification.
It isn’t law yet, but we cannot treat it as a mere policy draft either.
Many Pakistani tech companies already maintain strong governance practices because foreign clients demand it.
The policy isn’t a privacy law, it doesn’t tell private companies how to collect or use their customers’ data. Instead it focuses on something narrower but, in many respects, more consequential: government data. That distinction matters because government data rarely stays inside the government.
Across Pakistan, private companies build digital services for public agencies, host government systems, operate call centres, manage cloud infrastructure and process citizen information on the state’s behalf. Many businesses think of themselves as serving a government client; fewer recognise they’re becoming part of its data governance framework.
The finalised policy makes that explicit. Its obligations extend beyond ministries and departments to contractors, processors, concessionaires, grantees and other entities processing government data or performing public functions for the federal government. For many technology companies, compliance won’t begin with a regulator knocking, it begins with revised procurement requirements and contractual terms.
Pakistan’s privacy debate has largely been framed around one question: when will parliament finally pass a comprehensive data protection law? The finalised policy raises an equally important one that’s already here: how should organisations manage government-held information when governance obligations arrive through contracts rather than legislation?
The answer has practical consequences. The policy classifies government data by sensitivity and restricts where certain categories may be stored or processed. It tightens controls on cross-bo­­rder transfers of sensitive information and expects contractors to notify PDA, the body designated to enforce the framework, promptly following qualifying security incidents. Citizens also gain visibility into who accessed their data and why, making audit trails more than good internal practice, none of it dependent on a private-sector privacy law. It flows instead through the relationship between the state and the organisations it works with.
One detail from this week’s meeting stands out. PDA Chairman Dr Sohail Munir was clear the policy does not centralise government data or permit unrestricted sharing. Ownership stays with individual entities; a new mechanism, the WASL fra­mework, enables secure exchange between them based on classification and governance standards, not a single pooled database. That’s a more federated, realistic model than many expected, a sign the drafters were listening during consultation.
This reflects a broader shift in how governments think about data. For years, information collected by public bodies was treated as just another operational asset. The finalised policy takes a different view, describing government data as a strategic national asset held in trust for the people. This language shouldn’t be dismissed as symbolic. Organisations processing that data on the state’s behalf now assume responsibilities beyond delivering a contracted service; they are no longer simply vendors with access to sensitive information, but participants in a governance system built to protect it across its lifecycle.
Cabinet approval and gazette notification will start a phased rollout, with PDA-led capacity-buil­ding and governance arrangements, though detai­led timelines await a forthcoming National Data Strategy. That clock won’t stop at the ministries. Companies working with the government can exp­ect new requirements around data residency, security controls, breach reporting, access management and documentation as the rollout proceeds.
Many organisations will find the hard part isn’t technical safeguards, it’s knowing where government data resides, how it moves, and who has access, questions surprisingly hard to answer if never asked before.
There’s an opportunity hidden inside these obligations too, and the numbers aren’t small. Pakistan’s IT and IT-enabled services exports crossed $4.6 billion this past fiscal year, and nearly all of that revenue depends on the same kind of client trust the finalised policy now asks companies to demonstrate domestically.
Many Pakistani technology companies already maintain strong governance practices because international clients demand it; GDPR-compliant protections for Europe, security assessments for the US. The finalised policy means those investments can now serve domestic requirements too, let­­ting organisations build one programme that satisfies both international and public-sector demands.
That’s a more efficient way to think about compliance, and it reflects how regulation is evolving. Governments once relied mainly on legislation to shape corporate behaviour; increasingly, they do it through procurement, infrastructure requirements and technical standards. Companies waiting for a landmark privacy statute may find governance already arrived by other routes.
Pakistan’s Personal Data Protection Bill remains important; eventually the country will need a comprehensive legal framework governing personal data across both sectors. But waiting for that moment risks overlooking what has already happened this week.
The National Data Governance Policy doesn’t answer every privacy question in Pakistan, it was never meant to. What it signals is that data governance no longer waits for parliament. For much of the technology sector, it’s already arriving through the contracts they sign, the systems they build and the information they’re trusted to handle.
That is a change worth paying attention to, regardless of when Pakistan’s long-awaited privacy law finally arrives.
The writer is a technology lawyer specialising in data protection.

topic: Data Governance and Digital Transformation in Pakistan

summary: Pakistan has lacked a comprehensive data privacy law, with the Personal Data Protection Bill stalled since 2018, leading to an assumption of slow progress in data governance.

The Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) is fast-tracking the National Data Governance Policy 2026, which focuses primarily on government data and is nearing cabinet approval.

The new policy extends data governance obligations beyond government ministries to all private contractors, processors, and entities handling government data, imposing compliance through contractual terms rather than new legislation.

It classifies government data as a "strategic national asset," tightens controls on cross-border transfers, mandates breach reporting, and enables citizen visibility into data access, fostering a federated data exchange model (WASL framework) rather than centralization.
